title: Museum of Everyday Objects
description: Read wear, shape and context on invented museum cards to work out what ordinary things were for, then order object trios using receipts, archive notes, dig depths and serial numbers.

sections.title: Read the object
sections.description: Four object cards: use clues and separate evidence from inference.

sections.title: Place it in time
sections.description: Four trios: order objects using the dating clues on each card.

questions.prompt: Which job does this object most plausibly fit, based only on the physical clues on the card?
questions.context: Invented museum card: a wooden drum with fine mesh walls turns on a hand crank. Fine white dust coats the inside, the mesh has no scorch marks, and there are no water stains.
questions.explanation: Mesh, a turning drum and flour dust point to sifting. Scorching would suggest roasting, and water stains would suggest washing. None of those marks are present.

questions.prompt: What was this object most likely used for?
questions.context: Invented card: a lidded copper pan, 25 cm wide, with a perforated lid and a one-metre wooden handle. Ash lies inside, with no food residue or wax. The household inventory lists it beside bed linen.
questions.explanation: Ash, a long handle and its listing with bed linen suggest holding coals to warm bedding. No food or wax residue argues against cooking or candle work.

questions.prompt: Which use best fits the evidence recorded on this card?
questions.context: Invented card: a 3 kg iron block with a flat, polished base and a hinged wooden handle. A brown scorch mark and traces of starch cling to the base. The record notes it was heated on a stove.
questions.explanation: A polished flat base, heating, starch traces and cloth scorching all point to pressing wrinkles out of fabric. Grinding or crushing would not leave a polished base.

questions.prompt: Which statement about this object is an inference rather than something the object itself shows?
questions.context: Invented card: a brass tube, 14 cm long, with six evenly spaced holes. One end is worn smooth. It has no maker's mark.
questions.explanation: Length, hole spacing and wear can be observed directly. Claiming it was played at village dances goes beyond the object and needs other evidence, so it is an inference.

options.label: The tube has six evenly spaced holes
It was played at village dances

questions.prompt: Order these objects from earliest purchase to latest purchase.
questions.context: Invented town of Port Alder was founded in 1800; its centennial is 1900. Receipts: the tin pie safe was bought in the 9th year after founding. The copper kettle was bought in 1841. The slate board was bought 40 years before the centennial.
questions.explanation: The pie safe dates to 1809, the kettle to 1841, and the slate board to 1860 (1900 minus 40). Converting every clue to a year makes the order clear.

questions.prompt: Order these receipts from earliest to latest using the relative clues.
questions.context: Invented Eastfen Archive notes: the ice-box receipt is dated 3 years after the butter churn receipt. The milk cooler receipt is dated 2 years before the butter churn receipt.
questions.explanation: The cooler comes 2 years before the churn, and the ice-box comes 3 years after it. That gives cooler, churn, ice-box, with no absolute dates needed.

questions.prompt: Order these finds by when they were buried, oldest deposit first.
questions.context: Invented Lake Verrin dig, Pit 4. The layers are undisturbed, so deeper means buried earlier. Depths below the surface: iron key 85 cm, clay lamp 45 cm, bone needle 120 cm.
questions.explanation: In undisturbed layers, deeper deposits are older. The needle at 120 cm is oldest, then the key at 85 cm, then the lamp at 45 cm.

questions.prompt: Order these tools from earliest made to latest made using their stamped serial numbers.
questions.context: Invented Calder Tool Works numbered every tool in sequence, never reusing a number. The first series ended at 5,000, then a second series restarted at 1. Stamps: plane Second #12, awl First #3,905, hammer First #4,118.
questions.explanation: First-series tools come before any second-series tool. Within the first series, lower numbers came earlier: awl, then hammer, then the second-series plane.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All museum cards, towns, receipts, dig sites and tool makers are invented for this quiz. Each card supplies the clues you need. The quiz practices telling what an object shows apart from what a curator infers.

title: Before the First iPhone
description: Place dated records on the 2007 iPhone timeline, then spot the detail that breaks it. Uses verified milestones from the phonograph, Apollo 11 and the iPhone, plus invented archive cards.

sections.title: Before or After?
sections.description: Place events relative to the iPhone's 2007 milestones.

sections.title: Timeline Detective
sections.description: Find the detail that breaks the record.

questions.prompt: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969. How does that compare with the iPhone announcement?
questions.context: Apple announced the iPhone on January 9, 2007.

options.label: The landing came before the announcement
The landing came after the announcement
Both happened in the same decade

questions.explanation: 1969 is decades before 2007, so the Moon landing came well before the iPhone was announced.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates the iPhone announcement from its first US retail sale?

options.label: US stores sold it before Apple announced it
Announced January 9, 2007; first US sale June 29, 2007
Announced and first sold on the same day
First US sale in 2006, announcement in 2007

questions.explanation: The announcement came first in January 2007. Customers in the US could buy the phone about six months later, on June 29.

questions.prompt: Arrange these four real milestones from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: The phonograph patent (1878) precedes Apollo 11 (1969), which precedes the 2007 announcement and then the first US sale.

questions.prompt: Match each invented archive card to the period its date falls in.
questions.context: These cards are fictional. Use the real dates: announcement January 9, 2007; first US sale June 29, 2007.

right.label: Announced, not yet on US sale

questions.explanation: December 2006 precedes January 9. February falls between announcement and June 29. July and August are after sales began.

questions.prompt: Apollo 11 had three astronauts. Which one stayed in lunar orbit while the other two walked on the Moon?

options.label: All three walked on the Moon

questions.explanation: Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the Moon, while Collins stayed in lunar orbit.

questions.prompt: Which detail in this invented diary entry breaks the real timeline?
questions.context: Fictional diary: "March 15, 2007. Waited overnight in line at a US store and finally bought my first iPhone."

options.label: A US retail purchase on March 15, 2007

questions.explanation: The first US retail sale was June 29, 2007, so a March purchase conflicts with the record.

questions.prompt: Which detail in this invented TV listing breaks the Apollo 11 timeline?
questions.context: Fictional TV guide: "July 10, 1969, tonight: Apollo 11 astronauts walk on the Moon."

options.label: The date July 10, 1969 for a Moon walk

questions.explanation: Apollo 11 launched July 16 and landed July 20, 1969, so a Moon walk on July 10 cannot be right.

questions.prompt: A museum label discusses Edison's phonograph. Which wording stays within what the reference supports?

options.label: Patent issued February 19, 1878; exact build day uncertain

questions.explanation: The reference supports the February 19, 1878 patent date, but not a precise day for building the device.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data
Apple: first US iPhone retail launch
Library of Congress: cylinder phonograph history

note: This quiz focuses on verified milestones: the 2007 iPhone announcement and US sale, the Edison phonograph patent and Apollo 11. Diaries, blogs, receipts and listings are invented practice cards, not real records.

title: The Archive Has a Missing Page
description: Solve eight archive puzzles: order invented papers from their internal clues, work out what lost pages must have contained, and sort surviving sources from later interpretations.

sections.title: Three dossiers
sections.description: Order shuffled documents using only what they say about each other.

sections.title: Three gaps
sections.description: Decide what a missing page must have said.

sections.title: Case file
sections.description: Separate what is stated, what is forced, and what is unsupported.

questions.prompt: Order these invented ferry-guild papers from earliest to latest. Where the clues do not decide, either order is accepted.
questions.context: Invented dossier. Each paper's text refers to others: the Receipt pays the toll set in Notice N; Notice N says the toll is fixed as promised in Minute M; the Appeal protests the toll fixed in Notice N.
questions.explanation: Minute M comes first because Notice N cites its promise. Both the Receipt and the Appeal cite Notice N, but nothing places them relative to each other.

questions.prompt: Place these invented papers in date order. Every date is a whole calendar day in the same month.
questions.context: Ledger page: dated 9 May. Receipt: dated 12 May. Note: undated, 'written the day after the ledger page.' Memo: undated, written after the ledger page and before the receipt, on neither the ledger's date nor the note's date.
questions.explanation: The note falls on 10 May. The memo must lie between 9 and 12 May but cannot be 9 or 10, so it is 11 May.

questions.prompt: Order these invented orchard papers using their cross-references. Any order consistent with every clue is accepted.
questions.context: Charter: grants an orchard to the Dunmore sisters. Letter: accepts the terms of the charter. Map: drawn to the boundaries given in the charter. Report: compares the letter's acceptance with the map's boundaries.
questions.explanation: The Charter must come first because the Letter and Map both depend on it. The Report cites both of them, so it comes last; Letter and Map can swap.

questions.prompt: Which claim about the missing letter from B is directly established by Letter C's quotation?
questions.context: Invented orchard co-op. Letter C reads: 'You ask me to lend you seed grain until harvest. I will answer your request once I have counted my own stores.'
questions.explanation: Letter C reports that B asked for a seed loan. It does not say whether C agreed, what B offered, or when B's letter was dated.

options.label: B's letter asked C for a loan of seed grain
B's letter promised to repay with interest
C had already agreed to lend the seed
B's letter was written in the same week as C's

questions.prompt: Page 3 of this invented warden's file is lost. What must Page 3 have contained?
questions.context: Page 2 ends: 'The gate fee is recorded below, as agreed.' Page 4 begins: 'The fee of 6 coins named on page 3 was paid by the Weavers' Guild.'
questions.explanation: Page 4 explicitly says page 3 names a fee of 6 coins. It does not say who agreed to it or what the fee was charged per.

options.label: The Weavers' Guild promised to pay the gate fee
A gate fee of 6 coins was named
The fee was 6 coins for each person

questions.prompt: Page 5 of this invented ledger is lost. What amount must each of its entries have been?
questions.context: Page 4 closes with a running total of 40. Page 6 opens: 'Brought forward 46. Page 5 added three entries of equal amount, and nothing else changed the total.'
questions.explanation: The total rose from 40 to 46, a gain of 6. Three equal entries that account for the whole gain must each be 2.

questions.prompt: For each statement, say how the surviving invented diary page supports it.
questions.context: Surviving page: 'Today the potter Ila delivered twelve jars to the mill. Her cart wheel broke on the way, so the foreman Ugo sent a mule.'
questions.explanation: The jar count is stated outright. The wheel breaking on the way to the mill must precede the delivery. The page never says whose animal arrived first.

cells.label: The wheel broke before the delivery was complete
The mule reached the mill before Ila did

questions.prompt: Classify each invented item an historian might find about a harbor's trade.
questions.context: A primary source is made as part of people's lives at the time. A later interpretation explains the past from afterward. Use only the description given for each item.
questions.explanation: Items created during the events are primary sources, even if biased. Later summaries interpret evidence. A copy with no known origin cannot be classified from its description.

cells.label: A clerk's daily tally sheet written during the harbor's busy season
A textbook chapter written a century later summarizing the harbor trade
A merchant's private letter, written the week a shipment arrived late, complaining about the delay
A copied ledger page with no known author or date

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All archives, people, guilds and documents in this quiz are invented for the puzzles. Every answer follows from the clues given, not from outside knowledge.

title: Fact, Source Claim, or Interpretation?
description: Sort statements from an invented mill dossier into fact, source claim, or interpretation, decide what each source can prove, then choose labels the evidence actually supports.

questions.prompt: Match each statement from the Harlow Mill dossier to the label it deserves.
questions.context: Invented dossier: Harlow Mill, 1911. Documented fact: the record itself shows it. Source claim: a person asserts it in a source. Interpretation: a later reader infers a link between pieces of evidence.

left.label: The payroll ledger lists 140 names for March and 62 for June.
Diary text: "The hands left, so the mill closed."
A modern historian argues that wage cuts pushed workers out and doomed the mill.
The ledger's final entry is dated 30 June 1911.

questions.explanation: The ledger entries are directly recorded. The diary asserts a cause, and the historian infers a chain linking wages, departures, and closure from the evidence.

questions.prompt: An unsigned diary says workers leaving caused the mill closure. What does that excerpt alone establish?
questions.context: Invented case: the Harlow Mill diary has no signature and no other document confirms its claim.

options.label: That a writer offered this explanation of the closure
That worker departures definitely caused the closure
That the diarist was a mill clerk
That the owner agreed with the explanation

questions.explanation: A diary is evidence of what its writer believed or recorded. Causation needs corroboration, and an unsigned entry cannot confirm the writer's role or position.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a documented fact about the diary dossier, not an assumption?
questions.context: Invented dossier: the diary page is dated 3 June 1911 and contains the sentence "the hands are leaving." The writer is unknown.

options.label: Workers left because they feared the owner.
The 3 June 1911 page contains the sentence "the hands are leaving."
The mill failed as a result of worker departures.
The diarist worked in the mill office.

questions.explanation: What the page says is observable in the record. Motives, causes, and the writer's job all go beyond the page and would need further evidence.

questions.prompt: Match each source to what it can safely show on its own.
questions.context: All sources belong to the invented Harlow Mill dossier.

left.label: Undated photo of a padlocked mill gate

right.label: A scene, but not its date or cause

questions.explanation: Each source shows something direct, but explanations from the diarist or owner are perspectives. An undated photo cannot place the gate in time or give reasons.

questions.prompt: The owner's letter is clearly biased. How should a historian treat it?

options.label: Discard it, since biased sources are not evidence
Accept it as true because it was written at the time
Use it to see the owner's view, and test its claims against other records
Treat it as proof about every other mill

questions.explanation: A primary source may be biased or incomplete yet still reveals how its author saw events. Its claims need checking against other evidence.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for approaching an unfamiliar source, from first to last.

items.label: Observe: note what the item actually shows

questions.explanation: Source analysis starts with careful observation, then reflection on meaning, and finally questions for further research. This keeps what a record shows apart from inference.

questions.prompt: Which exhibit label best matches the evidence listed for the invented Harlow Mill?
questions.context: Evidence: the ledger shows 140 workers in March, 62 in June. The unsigned diary blames departures. The owner's dated 2 July letter says orders ran out after May.

options.label: Worker departures caused the Harlow Mill closure.
Payroll fell sharply; the diary blames departures and the owner cites lost orders, so cause remains unsettled.
The owner lied about lost orders to hide wage cuts.
The ledger proves the diary correct.

questions.explanation: The label reports the ledger drop as fact and presents the two explanations as competing claims. Neither the diary nor the letter alone settles causation.

questions.prompt: A draft label says rivals' arson is proven. Which rewrite fits the evidence?
questions.context: Invented case: an insurance record dates a fire at Dunmore Library to 1890. One newspaper says rivals were seen nearby that night. Nothing else addresses the cause.

options.label: Rivals set the Dunmore Library fire, as witnesses confirm.
The date of the fire is uncertain because newspapers can be biased.
An insurance record dates the fire to 1890; a newspaper reports rivals nearby, which suggests but does not prove arson.
The fire's cause is known because the newspaper named suspects.

questions.explanation: The record directly supports the date, while the newspaper report is one claim that hints at a cause. A careful label separates the two and avoids overreach.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: The Harlow Mill and Dunmore Library dossiers are invented for practice, with all evidence supplied in each question. They are not real historical records.

title: A City in Three Eras
description: Date invented archive records from the port city of Marlow Reach, match them to three eras, then work out what changed between eras and why.
note: Marlow Reach, its records and its eras are invented for this quiz. Every date and figure you need is supplied, so no outside knowledge of real cities is required.

sections.title: Streets and Records
sections.description: Date transport records and read them carefully.

sections.title: Buildings and Trades
sections.description: Match and compare the city's working life.

sections.title: What Changed and Why
sections.description: Use the evidence to explain change.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

questions.prompt: Match each dated transport record from invented Marlow Reach to the era in which it was created.
questions.context: Invented city eras: Era 1 is 1850–1879, Era 2 is 1880–1919, Era 3 is 1920–1959. Match by the date on each record.
questions.explanation: Each record's own date places it in an era. The horse tram stub and ferry bill both fall in Era 1, so two clues share one era.

questions.prompt: A memoir written in 1932 describes riding a horse tram in 1868. Which statement about the memoir is correct?
questions.context: Marlow Reach eras (invented): Era 1 is 1850–1879, Era 2 is 1880–1919, Era 3 is 1920–1959.

options.label: It was created in Era 3 but describes an Era 1 event
It was created in Era 1 and describes an Era 3 event
It was created and set entirely in Era 1
It was created in Era 2 and describes an Era 2 event

questions.explanation: A source is dated by when it was made, which can differ from the period it recalls. Memories written later are accounts, so they can be incomplete.

questions.prompt: Match each building or trade record from Marlow Reach to the era in which it was created.
questions.context: Invented eras: Era 1 is 1850–1879, Era 2 is 1880–1919, Era 3 is 1920–1959. Use each record's date.
questions.explanation: Dates settle each match. The permit from 1897 and the payroll from 1883 both belong to Era 2, so one era is used twice.

questions.prompt: Port ledgers show sailing-ship arrivals fell from 120 in Era 1 to 40 in Era 2. What fraction of the Era 1 figure was lost?
questions.context: Invented harbour ledger totals: Era 1 sailing arrivals 120; Era 2 sailing arrivals 40.
questions.explanation: The fall is 120 − 40 = 80 arrivals. Since 80 out of 120 simplifies to 2/3, two-thirds of the Era 1 figure was lost.

questions.prompt: Read the harbour table and choose which vessel type had the most arrivals in each era.
questions.context: Invented arrivals. Era 1: sailing 120, steam 10. Era 2: sailing 40, steam 160. Era 3: sailing 2, steam 90, motor 140.
questions.explanation: Compare the counts within each era: 120 sailing, then 160 steam, then 140 motor are the largest. The leading vessel type shifts each era.

questions.prompt: Which reason do these records directly give for where the grain elevator was sited?
questions.context: Invented records. 1883 minutes: rail spur reaches the east wharf. 1897 permit: elevator site is the east wharf, chosen so rail cars unload beside the ship berths. 1911 minutes: elevator cut hand-sack loading crews from 60 to 15.

options.label: It was beside the ferry dock
It was beside the rail spur and ship berths
It was near the horse tram depot
It was next to the cannery

questions.explanation: The permit itself states the rail-car and berth reasoning for the east wharf site. The other options appear nowhere in the supplied records.

questions.prompt: Order these Marlow Reach changes so each one comes after the change it depended on.
questions.context: Invented dependencies: streetcars needed a power station first. The elevator permit required the rail spur first. The crew reduction needed the elevator permitted first. The two chains are otherwise independent.
questions.explanation: Only the stated dependencies fix order: power before streetcars, and spur before elevator before crew cuts. The two chains can be interleaved in any way.

questions.prompt: The 1938 tram-closure minutes are summarized below. Which statement goes beyond the minutes, making it inference rather than evidence?
questions.context: Invented minutes, 1938: Tram lines close this year. Buses can use streets without rails. Track repairs cost more per mile than bus upkeep.

options.label: Track repairs cost more per mile than bus upkeep
Buses can use streets without rails
Most residents preferred buses to trams

questions.explanation: The minutes say nothing about resident opinion, so that claim is inference. The other three statements appear in the record itself.

title: How a Word Crossed Borders
description: Work through invented word dossiers: classify borrowing journeys, match words to contact settings, order dated records, and judge which word histories are certain or debated.

questions.prompt: Match each Lumeric word to the journey it took from Tarvani, using the dossier.
questions.context: Invented dossier. karbo: Tarvani 'karbo' (ledger) became Lumeric 'karbo' (ledger). vinto: Tarvani 'vinto' (lantern) became Lumeric 'vinto' (lantern). fire-wagon: Lumeric name for a train, built from Tarvani 'ignis-carra' (fire + wagon). moon-book: Lumeric calendar, from Tarvani 'luna-libra' (moon + book). salto: Tarvani 'salto' (jump) became Lumeric 'salto' (bonus pay).
questions.explanation: Words that keep sound and meaning are borrowed whole. Words rebuilt from translated parts are calques. A kept sound with a new meaning shows a shift.

questions.prompt: Which feature of the Tarvani word did Lumeric speakers not take over?
questions.context: Invented case: Lumeric 'hand-rinse' translates Tarvani 'mano-lava' (hand + wash) piece by piece.

options.label: The idea of combining hand and washing
The habit of naming an item by its action
The meaning of a thing used to rinse hands

questions.explanation: A piece-by-piece translation carries over structure and meaning but not the original sounds. Lumeric speakers built the word from their own parts.

questions.prompt: Which journey fits the Lumeric word 'kapheet'?
questions.context: Invented case: Tarvani 'kafeti' names a bitter leaf drink. Lumeric 'kapheet' names the same drink, sold by Tarvani merchants, spelled to fit Lumeric letters.
questions.explanation: Sound and meaning both arrived together, with only the spelling adapted. Meaning is unchanged and no parts were translated, so it counts as borrowed whole.

questions.prompt: Match each Lumeric word to the contact setting where its earliest records appear.
questions.context: Invented dossier. 'berth-tally' appears first only in Port Selu customs ledgers. 'rope-toll' appears first only in the same ledger series. 'slate-sum' appears first only in lesson notebooks of the Hall School.
questions.explanation: Earliest records point to the setting where each word was used. Two words share the harbor ledgers, one comes from school notebooks, and none are tied to the market.

questions.prompt: Using the rule, which word's earliest records all come from lesson notebooks?
questions.context: Rule: a setting is supported only if every earliest record is from it. ink-step: three notebooks. cable-fee: two customs ledgers, one notebook. ram-count: two market contracts. dock-sum: one customs ledger, one market contract.
questions.explanation: Only ink-step has records exclusively in notebooks. Cable-fee mixes ledgers and a notebook, so it fails the rule, and the other two lack notebooks.

questions.prompt: Order these events from earliest to latest using the dossier dates.
questions.context: Invented dates: Hall School opens 1431. 'slate-sum' in a notebook 1440. Tarvani ships first dock at Port Selu 1402. 'berth-tally' in a ledger 1415.

items.label: Tarvani ships first dock at Port Selu

questions.explanation: The dates run 1402, 1415, 1431, 1440. Contact at the harbor came first, and school words appear only after the school opened.

questions.prompt: Mark each word history as certain or debated under the dossier rule.
questions.context: Rule: certain means dated records in both languages show the direction of travel. Debated means the records cannot settle direction or independence.

cells.label: 'pilo': Tarvani glossary 1380 lists it; a 1410 Lumeric clerk's note says it came from Tarvani traders.
'dalu' (harbor): in both languages; Lumeric record 1390, Tarvani record 1440; nothing earlier in either.
'wenta' (wind-gap): Lumeric record 1400; a 1450 Tarvani glossary says maybe borrowed, maybe independent.

questions.explanation: Only 'pilo' has records on both sides showing direction. The earlier Lumeric date for 'dalu' does not prove direction, and the glossary for 'wenta' admits doubt.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates evidence from inference about this ledger entry?
questions.context: Invented record: a 1415 Port Selu ledger line writes 'berth-tally' beside the Tarvani phrase 'statio-numero'. No clerk's explanation survives.

options.label: Evidence: both phrases appear side by side. Inference: the clerk was translating the Tarvani phrase.
Evidence: the clerk translated the Tarvani phrase. Inference: both phrases appear side by side.
Evidence and inference are the same here, since the ledger is a primary source.
Neither is possible, because a ledger line cannot be used as evidence.

questions.explanation: A primary source shows what was written; why it was written is an interpretation. Observing the line comes first, then questioning and inferring.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: The languages Tarvani and Lumeric, their words, ports, schools and records are all invented, so every answer can be worked out from the dossier given. No real word histories are claimed.

title: Book, Place, Era: Connect the Three
description: Match invented books to their settings and story periods using clues inside short passages, then separate when a story is set from when it was published.

questions.prompt: Match each book to the place its passage clues point to.
questions.context: Invented library cards. Varnmouth is a harbor city, Oskerry a river market town, Tamsel a highland pottery village, Keld a coal-mining city. Brindle Cross is a farm crossroads. All books and places are fictional.

left.label: The Salt Ledger: customs sheds, gulls and a harbor bell
Lanterns on the Weir: a ferry to the weekly market
Quiet Kilns: kiln smoke above a village fair
The Last Tram to Keld: coal dust and a union hall

questions.explanation: Each passage describes features that its place card names: harbor, river market, highland pottery and coal mining. Brindle Cross has no matching clue.

questions.prompt: A passage says a letter postmarked Keld reached Anya while she unpacked in Varnmouth. Where is that scene set?
questions.context: Invented passage from the fictional novel Bell Over Varnmouth. Places named in a passage are not always where the action happens.
questions.explanation: Anya is in Varnmouth when the letter arrives. Keld is only where the letter was sent from, which is a mention rather than the scene.

questions.prompt: Match each book to the decade its dated clue shows. Some decades are shared.
questions.context: Each clue is a date stated inside the invented story, not the publication date.

left.label: The Salt Ledger: a new telegraph office opens in 1893
Bell Over Varnmouth: a lamp lighter retires in 1898
Lanterns on the Weir: a dance hall opens in 1926
Quiet Kilns: a tax roll dated 1766 is read aloud as current
The Last Tram to Keld: a depot wall calendar shows 1974

questions.explanation: The in-story dates give each decade. Two books share the 1890s, and no clue points to the 1950s.

questions.prompt: Which phrase lets a reader date the scene rather than place it?
questions.context: Invented passage: "Dalia left the highland kiln at Tamsel and, in the spring after the flood of 1763, carried bowls to market."

options.label: the spring after the flood of 1763

questions.explanation: The flood year anchors the scene in time. The kiln and Tamsel are place clues, while carrying bowls and leaving give no date.

questions.prompt: The Salt Ledger is set in 1893 and its copyright page says 1952. How many years apart are they?
questions.context: Invented catalog card: The Salt Ledger, depicted year 1893, published 1952.
questions.explanation: 1952 minus 1893 is 59. The gap shows the author wrote about a time well before the book appeared.

questions.prompt: For Lanterns on the Weir, mark each detail as story period or publication information.
questions.context: Invented card: story set in the 1920s in Oskerry; first published 1998; reissued with a new preface in 2001.

cells.label: A character mails a letter dated 1927
A dance hall opens in 1926 in the plot
A preface for a reissue is signed 2001

questions.explanation: Dates inside the plot describe the depicted world. Copyright pages and prefaces record when the book itself was produced.

questions.prompt: A reader says Quiet Kilns is from 1911, so its characters lived in 1911. Which correction fits the card?
questions.context: Invented card: Quiet Kilns, depicted period 1760s, published 1911, setting Tamsel.

options.label: The 1911 date is when the book appeared; the characters live in the 1760s.
The characters lived in 1911 and the book was written in the 1760s.
Both dates describe the story, since books depict their own publication year.
The card is contradictory, so neither date can be trusted.

questions.explanation: Publication date and depicted period are separate facts. The card records both without conflict, one for the book and one for the story.

questions.prompt: Which book has the largest gap between its depicted year and its publication year?
questions.context: Invented cards, depicted and published: The Salt Ledger 1893, 1952. Lanterns on the Weir 1926, 1998. Quiet Kilns 1766, 1911. The Last Tram to Keld 1974, 2009.
questions.explanation: The gaps are 59, 72, 145 and 35 years. Quiet Kilns has the largest at 145 years.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All books, places, passages and dates in this quiz are invented for the puzzles, so no outside knowledge is needed. Every answer comes from the clues given.

title: Trade Routes Behind a Breakfast
description: Read an invented harbor ledger. Trace breakfast ingredients through regions and arrival periods, decode cargo tags, and weigh the evidence for how foods spread.

sections.title: Plate to Port
sections.description: Trace four invented ingredients through the ledger.

sections.title: Why It Spread
sections.description: Choose the explanation the records actually support.

questions.prompt: Match each item on the invented Brindle Haven breakfast plate to the region where the ledger says it was grown.
questions.context: Invented Kestrel Strait ledger: Sunpears, Veshti Terraces, via Tolo Point, arrived Year 12. Lantern pepper, Veshti Terraces, via Tolo Point, Year 31. Reedsugar, Qanu Marsh Delta, via Verrin Mouth, Year 20. Ember-wheat, Dunmar Plain, via Ansel Quay, Year 5.
questions.explanation: Two items share the Veshti Terraces. Sharing a growing region does not mean sharing an arrival year, so each ledger line still needs its own reading.

questions.prompt: Match each item to the ledger period in which it first arrived at Brindle Haven.
questions.context: Same invented ledger: sunpears arrived Year 12, lantern pepper Year 31, reedsugar Year 20, ember-wheat Year 5. Periods are Early (Years 1–10), Middle (Years 11–25) and Late (Year 26 onward).
questions.explanation: Sunpears and reedsugar both land in the middle period, while wheat came first and pepper last. The plate combines items from different eras.

questions.prompt: Put the invented sunpear journey in an order that obeys the ledger rules. Any valid order is accepted.
questions.context: Rules from the invented ledger: the Tolo Point toll house stamped only cargo already carried down from the terraces. Ships accepted only stamped cargo. The Brindle Haven clerk copied cargo into the ledger after the ship arrived, and cooks plated jam after the ship arrived too.

items.label: Mule train carries crates to Tolo Point
Clerk copies the cargo into the ledger

questions.explanation: Picking, carrying, stamping and sailing form a fixed chain. The ledger copy and the plating both follow the ship's arrival, but neither rule orders them against each other.

questions.prompt: Decode each cargo tag from the ledger and choose which ingredient it labels.
questions.context: Invented tag rule: the letter is the first letter of the departure port (Ansel Quay, Tolo Point, Verrin Mouth), and the number is the arrival year at Brindle Haven. Use the ledger lines from the earlier tasks.
questions.explanation: Two goods left from Tolo Point, so the letter alone cannot separate them. The arrival year does: 12 is sunpears and 31 is lantern pepper.

questions.prompt: Which explanation fits all three invented records for sunpear jam becoming common in Brindle Haven?
questions.context: Year 13: the Tolo Point toll fell from 6 coins to 3 per crate. Sunpear crates landed: 40 in Year 12, 90 in Year 14. Jam price per jar: 8 coins in Year 12, 5 coins in Year 14.

options.label: A lower toll cut costs, so more crates arrived and jam got cheaper
Sunpear orchards were planted inside Brindle Haven
A law required every household to buy jam

questions.explanation: Only the toll cut, rising crate counts and the falling jar price appear together in the records. The other options add events that the records never mention.

questions.prompt: Using these invented bakery records, why did reedsugar replace honey in most recipes?
questions.context: Honey cost 9 coins per jar in Year 18 and 14 coins in Year 22 after a drought thinned the harvest. Reedsugar syrup stayed at 4 coins per jar. Recipes using reedsugar: 3 of 12 bakeries in Year 18, 10 of 12 in Year 22.

options.label: Honey grew costlier while reedsugar stayed cheap and steady
Reedsugar reached the port before ember-wheat did
Reedsugar was grown in Brindle Haven gardens
Bakers were banned from using honey

questions.explanation: The bakery counts rose exactly while honey's price climbed and reedsugar's did not. Nothing here shows a ban, local growing, or an earlier arrival.

questions.prompt: Which link in these invented records best explains how pepper relish reached inns beyond Brindle Haven?
questions.context: Year 31: Dock Kitchen gave free relish spoonfuls to sailors and listed their names. Year 33 crew lists show three of those listed sailors later running inns in Marl, Pell and Dunn. Inn menus listing relish: none in Year 30, two (Marl, Pell) in Year 33, five in Year 36.

options.label: Sailors who sampled it later ran inns in nearby towns
The Tolo Point toll fell for lantern pepper
Marl and Pell grew lantern pepper themselves
Inn owners were required to serve it

questions.explanation: The tasting list, the crew lists naming the same sailors and the later menus form a connected chain. It is the best-supported link, not proof. The records give no toll change, local pepper growing, or serving requirement.

questions.prompt: What can a historian responsibly conclude from this invented ledger alone about reedsugar labor?
questions.context: The merchant's clerk wrote the Qanu delta entries. They list reedsugar cutters as 'bonded workers' with no wages recorded. No cutter's own account survives in the archive.

options.label: Cutters were fairly paid for their work
The merchant record shows bonded labor without recorded wages, but not the cutters' own experiences
Nothing at all can be learned from the ledger

questions.explanation: A record made as part of daily business is evidence, yet it may be biased or incomplete. Separate what it shows from what it cannot tell us.

title: Two Sources, One Event
description: Compare invented pairs of historical accounts, label each pair as a conflict, complement, or different scale, then pick the follow-up question a historian should ask.

sections.title: Name the relationship
sections.description: Classify how two accounts relate.

sections.title: Ask the next question
sections.description: Choose a useful follow-up for each pair.

questions.prompt: Match each pair of accounts to the relationship it shows.
questions.context: All sources here are invented practice records from the made-up town of Harrowmere. Conflict means they cannot both be right. Complement means they add different pieces. Different scale means they measure different spans or groups.

left.label: Customs log: 'Gale winds blew from midnight to noon.' Diary: 'The storm kept us indoors three days.'
Census: '1,200 residents lived in Harrowmere in 1850.' Letter: 'Our street had 30 households that year.'

questions.explanation: The log measures peak wind while the diary describes how long life was disrupted. The census covers the whole town, the letter one street. Neither pair contradicts itself.

questions.prompt: Match each of these two invented pairs to the relationship it shows.
questions.context: Again these Harrowmere records are invented for practice. Decide whether each pair clashes, fills in missing pieces for each other, or measures different scales.

left.label: Clinic record: 'Fourteen workers treated for burns after the mill fire.' Foreman's note: 'The fire began in the dye shed.'
Ferry register: '40 passengers boarded the 8 a.m. crossing on 12 June.' Pilot's letter: '25 passengers boarded the 8 a.m. crossing on 12 June.'

questions.explanation: The clinic record gives the human toll and the note gives the fire's origin, so together they say more. The ferry counts cover the same crossing but disagree.

questions.prompt: Which added detail would turn an apparent disagreement into a true conflict?
questions.context: Invented case: a harbor log says fog lasted two hours. A diary says fog lasted all week.

options.label: Both writers described the same harbor on the same morning, but gave different durations.
The diary writer lived several miles inland.
The log was written in ink.
The diary is longer than the log.

questions.explanation: A true conflict needs the same place, time, and thing measured. Without matching scope, the accounts may simply describe different spans or locations.

questions.prompt: Which statement in this entry is an inference rather than what the record shows?
questions.context: Invented diary entry: 'The mayor left the meeting at noon, face red, and I think he panicked.'
questions.explanation: The first three are observations the writer reports. The mayor's inner state is the writer's interpretation, which needs other evidence to support it.

questions.prompt: A harbor log reports no deaths in a storm; a widow's letter says her brother never returned. What should a historian ask next?
questions.context: Both records are invented. The log covers the night of the storm.

options.label: Which writer is more trustworthy overall?
Did the log count only ship crews, and was her brother counted among them?
Can the letter be ignored because it is personal?

questions.explanation: The two may count different groups. Checking what the log covered tests whether this is a real conflict or a mismatch in scope.

questions.prompt: A mill payroll lists 30 workers; a strike leaflet says hundreds were locked out. What is the best next question?
questions.context: Both documents are invented and describe the same week. Best here means the question that checks whether they measure the same thing.

options.label: Why not discard the leaflet since it takes a side?
Why not trust the payroll since it is official?
Do both sources count the same group, such as payroll employees versus all affected townspeople?
Which source has the nicer wording?

questions.explanation: Payrolls and leaflets often count different groups. Establish what each counted before deciding that either number is wrong.

questions.prompt: A surveyor's note dates a well to 1851; a neighbor's letter mentions drawing water from it in a dry year. What next?
questions.context: Invented records. They do not contradict each other. The letter gives no year.

options.label: Which other records, such as deeds or tax entries, could date the dry year and the well's use?
Which of the two is the correct one?
Who deserves credit for the well?
Should the neighbor's letter be dropped for lacking a date?

questions.explanation: The accounts fit together, so the useful move is to find independent records that date the dry year and fill the gap.

questions.prompt: A passenger list shows departure on 3 May; a diary says 'we sailed on the 5th.' What should a historian ask?
questions.context: Invented records about one ship. Neither source says whether a delay occurred.

options.label: Why not average the dates to 4 May?
Why not discard the diary because it is private?
Does the list record the scheduled departure while the diary records when the ship actually sailed?

questions.explanation: The list and diary may record different moments: the plan versus the event. Clarifying what each date refers to comes before declaring a conflict.

title: Whose Voice Is Missing?
description: Answer six research dilemmas and two project tradeoffs about which sources you would seek first, then see where your style falls between close-up and wide-angle, and between written record and spoken memory.

sections.description: Six research dilemmas about the first source you would seek.

sections.title: Project Tradeoffs
sections.description: Two choices between breadth and depth.

dimensions.description: Whether you tend to begin with one person or object in detail, or with patterns across many sources.
Whether you tend to trust and seek documents first, or people's recalled stories first.

questions.prompt: You are studying a flooded river town. Which source would you seek first?
questions.context: All towns, people and records in this quiz are invented for the exercise.
questions.explanation: There is no right first source. A diary or descendant's account is close-up, while a ledger or map shows wider patterns. Written and spoken sources capture different things.

options.label: A resident's diary from the flood week
A merchant's ledger showing losses across the district
A survey map marking which streets were underwater
A descendant's account of what their family was told

questions.prompt: The date of a bridge repair is unclear. What would you check first?
questions.context: The bridge belongs to an invented town called Millbrook Crossing.
questions.explanation: Each route is reasonable. Choosing one worker's letter or one family's memory is a close-up approach, while comparing many records or neighbors gives a wider view.

options.label: One repair worker's letter describing the job
Several years of county repair records side by side
A recorded interview with a retired crew member's family
Recollections gathered from many neighbors at a meeting

questions.prompt: Rank these starting points for a history of a neighborhood bakery, from first choice to last.
questions.context: The bakery is an invented example that opened decades ago.
questions.explanation: Your ranking shows which kinds of evidence attract you first. None is wrong, and a full project would eventually use several of them.

items.label: Business directories listing the bakery across decades
A recorded memory from a longtime customer
Stories collected from a neighborhood gathering

questions.prompt: Match each research situation to the approach you would try first.
questions.context: Several approaches can be used more than once.
questions.explanation: These pairings reveal habits. Zooming in or surveying widely changes scale, while paper trails and spoken memories change the kind of voice you hear.

left.label: A puzzling gap in the story
A new volunteer asks where to begin

right.label: Zoom in on one person's experience

questions.prompt: Where do you land when choosing a lens for a local history project?
questions.explanation: Neither end is better. Close-up work finds texture and detail, while wide-angle work finds patterns and scale.

questions.prompt: A written record and a family story seem to differ. Where does your curiosity lean first?
questions.context: Both are evidence. Observing what each one actually says comes before deciding how to explain the difference.
questions.explanation: A record shows what someone wrote down, and a memory shows what someone carried forward. Careful researchers observe both before inferring.

questions.prompt: You have one month for an invented flood-history project. Which plan appeals most?
questions.explanation: Each plan trades breadth for depth differently. Deep study of few sources and quick coverage of many both produce useful but different history.

options.label: Study three diaries closely, line by line
Skim fifteen ledgers for district-wide totals
Hold two long interviews with family members

questions.prompt: For a small exhibit about the invented flood, which centerpiece would you build?
questions.explanation: The centerpiece shapes what visitors notice. Exhibits can feature one voice or many, and documents or testimony, but no single form shows everything.

options.label: One annotated page from a single document
A timeline wall built from dated records
A listening booth featuring one person's recorded story
A community map pinned with many recollections

title: Time Capsule Packing Dilemma
description: Choose, match, rank and cut items for a box meant for future readers, then see where your picks fall on two scales: practical to personal and everyday to rare.

sections.title: Packing the box
sections.description: Six choices about what future readers should find.

sections.title: Making cuts
sections.description: The box is too full. Remove items.

dimensions.description: Whether you lean toward items that explain how things worked or items that carry feelings and relationships.
Whether you lean toward ordinary daily objects or unusual, one-off pieces.

questions.prompt: The capsule has space for exactly one more item. Which goes in?
questions.explanation: There is no right answer. A letter leans personal, a transit map or receipt leans practical, and a school bulletin sits in the everyday middle.
questions.context: Invented scenario: a community box will be opened in fifty years by readers who never met you.

options.label: A handwritten letter to whoever opens the box
A folded transit map of your city
A school bulletin listing this week's events
A household receipt showing what a week of shopping cost

questions.prompt: Next slot. Which small paper item would you slip into the box?
questions.explanation: These items sort along both axes: a shopping list is personal and ordinary, a timetable practical and ordinary, a notice practical and rare, a pressed leaf personal and rare.

options.label: A bus timetable from this season
A pressed leaf from a tree you love
A printed notice for a once-only city event

questions.prompt: The box fits one photograph. Which scene would you print?
questions.explanation: Photographs can document or connect. A noon street scene documents daily life; a milestone portrait is personal and special; an eclipse crowd is public and rare.

options.label: A busy street at ordinary midday
A family dinner table on a normal night
A crowd watching a rare sky event
A portrait with a friend at a big milestone

questions.prompt: Match each object to the reason you would pack it. Reasons may repeat.
questions.explanation: Your reasons move your two scales. Explaining routines is practical and everyday, memory is personal, and surprise or meaning pushes toward rare.
questions.context: Objects: a monthly transit pass, a hand-drawn birthday card, a ticket stub from a one-time lantern festival, and a repair guide for a kitchen tap.

right.label: Means a lot to one person but is a rarity

questions.prompt: Slide toward the kind of object that would best show a future reader today.
questions.explanation: Left favors common objects that many people used; right favors distinctive pieces. Both can tell a story, so this just places your instinct.

questions.prompt: Rank these for the top layer of the box, the first thing readers see.
questions.explanation: Your top picks weigh most on your two scales. Schedules are practical and common, thank-you notes personal and common, festival programs practical and rare, tokens personal and rare.

items.label: A daily schedule for a local school
A program from a one-time festival
A cherished token with a private story

questions.prompt: The box is too heavy. Which item do you take out first?
questions.explanation: Cuts reveal what feels less essential. Removing a timetable leans personal; removing a note leans practical; removing a rare stub leans everyday; removing a receipt leans rare.

questions.prompt: One final cut before sealing. Which item comes out?
questions.explanation: Each removal nudges your scales away from what you drop. Dropping a how-to sheet leans personal and rare, while dropping a rare keepsake leans practical and everyday.

options.label: A how-to sheet for a household routine
A note recording a family joke
A keepsake from a once-in-a-lifetime trip
A printed flyer for a rare city event

dimensions.description: Authoritative museums lean on curator expertise and fixed interpretation; participatory ones invite visitors to add stories and shape meaning.

questions.prompt: One room is left in your small town museum. Which feature fills the last gallery?
questions.explanation: There is no right answer. A talk space invites visitors in, while a timeline or artifact hall leans on curated presentation.
questions.context: All museums in this quiz are invented for play. Budget is tight, so only one feature fits.

A loud artifact hall full of showpieces

Curator label with a space for visitor replies beside it
Labels that connect each object to faraway trade or travel

A climate-controlled case for one rare object
A touring exhibit borrowed from a distant museum

questions.prompt: Rank these four Saturday programs from the one you would schedule first to the one you would schedule last.

items.label: Expert lecture on regional digging finds
Pen-pal exhibit with a museum abroad
Guided world-comparison tour led by curators

title: The Festival Calendar Has a Gap
description: Fill in invented town calendars of festivals and harvests using before-and-after clues, then settle disagreements between two archive records.

questions.prompt: Place each invented event in its month using the clue.
questions.context: In the invented town of Veloria, one event happens in each of March, April and May. Clue: the lantern fair follows the grain count but comes before the river market.
questions.explanation: The lantern fair sits between the other two events, so the grain count is first, the lantern fair second and the river market last.

questions.prompt: Four invented events fill four months, one per month. Find each event's month.
questions.context: Months: June, July, August, September. Clues: the barley harvest is neither first nor last. Kite day is the month immediately before the boat race. The salt count comes after the boat race.
questions.explanation: The boat race cannot be September, because the salt count must follow it. If kite day is July and the boat race August, the salt count is September and barley falls in June, which is first. So kite day is June, the boat race July, barley August and the salt count September.

questions.prompt: Each invented festival marks one harvest. Work out the months and the Ferry day harvest.
questions.context: Festivals: Seed swap, Lantern fair, Ferry day, one each in October, November, December. Harvests: rye, flax, pears, one per festival. Clues: the flax festival is in October. The Lantern fair is neither the flax nor the pears festival. The rye festival is before the pears festival. Ferry day is not the flax festival.
questions.explanation: Lantern fair must be rye. Flax is October, so rye is November and pears December. Ferry day cannot be flax, so it is pears, leaving the Seed swap as flax.

questions.prompt: The calendar has an empty month. Place the three events and find the gap.
questions.context: Months: April, May, June, July. Three invented events fall in three different months. The lantern fair is exactly two months after the grain count. The river market is after the lantern fair.
questions.explanation: The grain count must be April: a later start leaves no room for a market after the fair. That puts the fair in June, the market in July, and May empty.

questions.prompt: Two invented records disagree. Decide the months and which record must be corrected.
questions.context: Rule: a receipt stamped on the day outranks later copies. Ledger (copied later): lantern fair in May, river market in June. Receipt: river market stamped in May. Diary: the lantern fair was the month before the river market. Assume the diary holds unless a receipt contradicts it.
questions.explanation: The stamped receipt fixes the river market in May. The diary then puts the lantern fair in April. The later ledger copy contradicts the receipt, so it needs correcting.

questions.prompt: Use the dated records to settle the barley harvest date, the gap, and the faulty record.
questions.context: Rule: records made at the time outrank later summaries. Field log (made at the time): barley harvest began August 3. Tally stamp (made at the time): salt count August 20. Summary (written later): barley harvest was 12 days before the salt count.
questions.explanation: The two same-time records agree: August 3 and August 20 are 17 days apart. The later summary implies August 8, so it is the record in error.

cells.label: Days from harvest to salt count

questions.prompt: Arrange these invented events in any order that respects every record.
questions.context: Records: the sheep fair is before the shearing count. The shearing count is before the wool market. Ink day is before the wool market. The wool market is before the winter tally.
questions.explanation: Only the stated before-and-after links matter. Ink day and the sheep fair can swap places, as long as the market follows both the count and Ink day.

questions.prompt: Which statement is an inference rather than something the record directly shows?
questions.context: Invented ledger entry: "Lantern oil bought, 40 jars, 3 March."
questions.explanation: The entry shows a purchase, a quantity and a date. Saying the fair was held that day goes beyond it, since oil could be bought well before an event.

options.label: The ledger lists 40 jars of oil bought on 3 March.
The lantern fair must have been held on 3 March.
The entry gives a quantity of jars.

questions.prompt: Each carrier takes exactly one good. Which carrier takes each good?
questions.context: Invented route. Carriers: a cart and two boats, Ember and Reed. Goods: ink, glass, seed. Clues: glass never rides the cart; ink rides a boat; ink is not on Reed.
questions.explanation: Ink must ride a boat that is not Reed, so Ember. Glass cannot use the cart, so it takes Reed, leaving seed for the cart.

questions.prompt: Four carriers each take one good. Choose the good for every carrier.
questions.context: Invented route. Goods: lamps, salt, tiles, wool. Clues: tiles avoid the Mule and Sled; lamps avoid the Sled and Cart; wool avoids the Barge, Mule and Cart; salt avoids the Cart and Mule.
questions.explanation: Wool is left only the Sled. Salt then has only the Barge, tiles must take the Cart, and lamps end up on the Mule.

questions.prompt: Every carrier takes one load and no load may exceed capacity. Which carrier takes each load?
questions.context: Invented route. Capacities: Cart 6, Skiff 4, Mule 3, Raft 3. Skiff and Raft float. Loads: Bales 6, Jars 4, Reels 3, Nets 2. Reels must not float.
questions.explanation: Only the Cart holds Bales and only the Skiff is left for Jars. Reels cannot float, so they take the Mule, leaving Nets for the Raft.

questions.prompt: Use the weight clues. Which good does each carrier take?
questions.context: Invented route. Carriers: Cart, boat Kite, boat Loon. Goods: ink, glass, seed. Clues: the Cart takes the heaviest good; glass is lighter than ink; ink is lighter than seed; Kite takes the lightest good.
questions.explanation: Glass is lighter than ink, which is lighter than seed, so seed is heaviest and glass lightest. Cart gets seed, Kite gets glass and Loon gets ink.

questions.prompt: Fill each position on the route with the stop visited there.
questions.context: Invented route with four stops: Mill, Ford, Quarry, Harbor. Clues: Harbor is the last stop; Mill comes directly after Ford; Quarry is visited before Mill.
questions.explanation: Ford and Mill must be adjacent, and Quarry needs to precede Mill. That only works as Quarry, Ford, Mill, with Harbor closing the route.

questions.prompt: Choose the visit position for every stop on this second route.
questions.context: Invented route with four stops: Chalk Bridge, Dye Yard, Eel Landing, Fort Gate. Clues: Fort Gate is before Dye Yard; Dye Yard is before Chalk Bridge; Eel Landing is the stop directly before Chalk Bridge.
questions.explanation: Chalk Bridge needs Fort Gate, Dye Yard and Eel Landing all before it, so it is 4th. Eel Landing is then 3rd, leaving Fort Gate 1st and Dye Yard 2nd.

questions.prompt: Order the dock jobs so every ledger rule holds. Any valid order counts.
questions.context: Invented dock ledger rules: weigh crates before stacking; pack glass in straw before stacking; stack before tying the tarp; tie the tarp before signing the manifest.
questions.explanation: Weighing and packing are both prerequisites for stacking, in either order. Stacking then leads to the tarp and finally the signed manifest.

questions.prompt: Which loading plan obeys every rule and capacity limit?
questions.context: Invented rules: Cart holds up to 3 units, Boat up to 5. Ink is 2 units, glass 2, seed 3. Glass never rides the cart; seed must ride the boat.
questions.explanation: Seed and glass fill the boat at 5 units, leaving ink on the cart at 2. Other plans put glass on the cart, seed off the boat or overload the boat.

options.label: Boat: seed and glass. Cart: ink.
Boat: seed and ink. Cart: glass.
Boat: glass and ink. Cart: seed.
Boat: seed, ink and glass. Cart: nothing.

title: What the Railroad Changed
description: Order dated records from four invented railroad-town archives, then separate documented changes from interpretation, including displacement and labor costs.

sections.title: Order the Records
sections.description: Use each dossier to sequence what happened.

sections.title: Check the Evidence
sections.description: Separate what records show from what people infer.

questions.prompt: Order these Harlow Ford records from earliest to latest using the ledger dates.
questions.context: Invented town archive. Ledger: depot opened 4 May 1881; grain warehouse permit stamped 19 Aug 1881; telegraph office hired a second clerk 11 Nov 1881; weekly paper's first rail-delivered edition 2 Feb 1882.
questions.explanation: Dated ledger entries give a documented sequence: depot, warehouse, telegraph clerk, then newspaper. Sequence shows order only, not why each change happened.

items.label: Telegraph office hires a second clerk

questions.prompt: Order these Alder Mills records from earliest to latest, including the costs borne by tenants and laborers.
questions.context: Invented dossier. Survey stakes set on tenant farms 3 Mar 1890; eviction notices to tenants 20 Jun 1890; tenant letter describing the move 2 Aug 1890; first construction payroll 14 Sep 1890; station opened 2 Apr 1891.
questions.explanation: The records show tenants were notified and moved before the first payroll and the station opening. Growth in town came alongside displacement, not instead of it.

items.label: Survey stakes set on tenant farms

questions.prompt: Using the relative timings supplied, order these Mill Rapids events from earliest to latest.
questions.context: Invented dossier. The depot opened Monday 6 April 1896. The hotel permit was stamped 12 days before that. The first freight run came 21 days after opening. Ferry deckhands were laid off 9 days after the freight run.
questions.explanation: Hotel permit: 25 March. Depot: 6 April. Freight run: 27 April. Layoffs: 6 May. Computing dates from the record keeps the order documented rather than guessed.

questions.prompt: Order the Prairie Siding events. Every ordering that respects the dossier's stated before/after clues is accepted.
questions.context: Invented dossier. The deed was signed before the track crew camp was built. The wage book's first page cites the camp as already standing. The wage book was open before the first train ran. The boarding house's first guest entry names the train as how the guest arrived.
questions.explanation: The clues form a chain: deed, camp, wage book, first train, guest entry. Each link comes from a stated clue rather than an assumption.

questions.prompt: Which claim about Harlow Ford needs more evidence than the supplied records provide?
questions.context: Invented records: depot opened May 1881. A price table shows wheat at 60 cents a bushel in 1880 and 66 cents in 1882. A farmer's diary says the neighboring county's harvest failed in 1881.
questions.explanation: The records document the opening and the prices. They do not isolate the rail link as the cause, since the neighboring failed harvest could also have affected prices.

options.label: The rail link caused the wheat price rise.
Wheat was listed at 66 cents in 1882.
A diary reports a failed harvest nearby in 1881.

questions.prompt: Classify each statement about Cedar Landing as observed in the records, an inference, or unsupported.
questions.context: Invented dossier: a notice register lists six tenant families served notices. Company minutes call the line 'cleared'. Payroll shows laborers at 90 cents a day, foremen at 2 dollars. No compensation records survive.
questions.explanation: Register and payroll show facts directly. 'Cleared' supports only an inference about attitudes. With no payment records, a claim of fair compensation has no support.

cells.label: Managers treated the removals as routine business.
Every displaced family received fair payment.
Laborers earned less per day than foremen.

questions.prompt: Match each causal claim to the missing record that would test it most directly.
questions.context: Invented claims about the town of Wren Crossing. Each claim is currently only asserted, not documented.
questions.explanation: Each claim needs a record measuring the thing it names: shipping costs, arrivals, circulation, or ferry use, compared before and after the link.

left.label: Rail cut the cost of shipping grain.
Rail drew new laborers who stayed in town.
Rail delivery grew the paper's readership.
Rail took passengers away from the ferry.

right.label: Freight rates before and after opening
Boarding register with arrival dates and jobs
Subscriber ledger by year and route

questions.prompt: What do the shop counts suggest about the rail link's effect?
questions.context: Invented data over the same ten years. Town A, with a rail link, grew from 40 to 52 shops. Town B, with no link, grew from 25 to 32 shops.
questions.explanation: A grew 30 percent and B grew 28 percent. The gap is small, so these counts alone do not show the rail link caused A's growth.

options.label: Rail clearly caused Town A's shop growth.
Both towns grew similarly, so the link's effect is not shown.
The absence of rail harmed Town B's shops.
Comparing towns can never tell us anything.

title: Street Names: Clue or Overreach?
description: Judge what a place name can really tell you about the past. Choose safe inferences from invented street cases, then flag overreach and match each question to a record that could answer it.

sections.title: Reading the clue
sections.description: What does a name, plus any supplied record, actually support?

sections.title: Spotting overreach
sections.description: Flag claims that go too far and pick better evidence.

questions.prompt: Using only the name, which inference about Mill Road is safest?
questions.context: Invented town of Alderford: Mill Road runs beside the Larch River. No map, deed, photograph or written record is supplied.
questions.explanation: A name is a clue, not proof. It makes a mill connection plausible, but location, dates and operation need maps, deeds or other records.

options.label: A mill definitely operated on this exact spot.
A mill may be connected to the area, but other records are needed to confirm it.
River power ran the mill for over a century.
The mill's owner personally named the road.

questions.prompt: The name and the ledger together support which statement?
questions.context: Invented dossier: Ferry Lane in Brandel ends at a river bridge built in 1931. An 1890 ledger lists ferry fees collected at the foot of Ferry Lane.
questions.explanation: The dated ledger supports a ferry service there in 1890. It says nothing about when service ended or why the bridge or lane got their names.

options.label: A ferry was operating near the lane's foot in 1890.
The ferry kept running until the 1931 bridge opened.
The bridge was named after the old ferry.
The town government owned the ferry.

questions.prompt: Match each invented street case to how well its evidence supports the stated claim.
questions.context: All streets are in the invented city of Tolvane.
questions.explanation: A dated survey directly supports the bridge claim. A bare name makes an orchard plausible only, while royal visits and present-day quarrying need separate evidence.

left.label: Orchard Way, name only: an orchard once grew nearby
Bridge Street, an 1902 survey shows a bridge at its east end: a bridge stood there in 1902
Kings Road, name only: a monarch once stayed on it
Quarry Street, an 1880 map labels a quarry beside it: the quarry still works today

questions.prompt: What does the current name Harbor Avenue show about street use in the 1850s?
questions.context: Invented city of Marrow Bay: council minutes say Tin Street was renamed Harbor Avenue in 1960 to simplify mail sorting.
questions.explanation: The present name dates from 1960 and was chosen for postal reasons, so it cannot directly describe the 1850s. The older name Tin Street might be a clue instead.

options.label: Nothing directly, because it was assigned in 1960 for mail reasons.
Harbor activity filled the street in the 1850s.
Sailors chose the name in the nineteenth century.
The tin trade had ended before 1850.

questions.prompt: Order this source-analysis routine from first step to last when studying an old street record.
questions.context: Think of a dated map showing a street label.
questions.explanation: Start by observing what the record plainly shows, then reflect on what it may mean, and finally question what is missing or uncertain.

items.label: Question what the record leaves out
Observe what the record plainly shows
Reflect on what it might mean

questions.prompt: Which source could actually test the pamphlet's claim about annual executions?
questions.context: Invented village of Pell Hollow: a modern pamphlet says Gallows Hill Road hosted executions every year for 200 years. The only evidence given is the road's name.
questions.explanation: Dated court and county records are contemporary documents that could confirm or contradict executions. Repeated pamphlets, signs and polls only repeat the story.

options.label: Dated court sentencing records and county accounts
Another modern pamphlet repeating the story
A poll of which story residents like best

questions.prompt: Label each name-based claim as a cautious clue or an overreach.
questions.context: Invented town of Eddling. Salt Lane and Weaver Court are known by name only, with no other records.
questions.explanation: Names can hint at associated activity. Claims about who lived there, or what every house held, go beyond a name and need specific records.

cells.label: Salt Lane: salt may have been handled or traded nearby
Salt Lane: its founders were all salt merchants
Weaver Court: weaving may have been linked to the area
Weaver Court: every house had a loom in 1850

questions.prompt: Match each question about an invented street to the record type that could best answer it.
questions.context: Invented city of Orrin Vale holds council minutes, an 1875 trade directory and land deeds.
questions.explanation: Minutes record official decisions, a directory lists trades operating in a year, and a deed shows who held a lot. Each source answers different questions.

left.label: On what date did the council formally adopt the name Elm Terrace?
Which trades operated on the street in 1875?
Who owned a given lot when the road was laid out?
Did the council vote to rename a street after a person?
