note: All towns, streets, ledgers, surveys and records in this quiz are invented for practice. They are not real local histories, so use them to practice reasoning rather than to learn real street origins.

title: Made by Hand: Order the Steps
description: Work through invented paper mill, weaving shed and print shop records. Put craft stages in a valid order, match tools to stages, and check what a record really shows.

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps at Linden Ford mill. Any order that obeys every foreman's rule counts.
questions.context: Linden Ford is an invented mill. Foreman's rules: beating needs fibers already soaked. A sheet is lifted only from beaten pulp and only with the screen frame ready. Pressing needs a lifted sheet. Drying comes after pressing.
questions.explanation: Soaking must precede beating, and beating plus the ready frame must precede lifting. Pressing then follows lifting, and drying follows pressing. Preparing the frame can happen at any earlier point.

items.label: Lift a sheet on the screen

questions.prompt: Which statement about this entry is an inference, not something the entry itself shows?
questions.context: Invented day-book entry, Linden Ford: "Tuesday. Forty sheets lifted. Vat cold. Press jammed after noon."
questions.explanation: The entry records the sheet count, the cold vat and the jam. Saying the jam cost the mill money goes beyond the record and needs more evidence.

options.label: Forty sheets were lifted on Tuesday.
The press jam cost the mill money that week.

questions.prompt: When does drying begin at the invented Ash Row mill?
questions.context: Ash Row runs five stages back to back from 06:00 with no waiting: soak 6 hours, beat 2 hours, lift 1 hour, press 3 hours, dry 8 hours.
questions.explanation: Soaking ends at 12:00, beating at 14:00, lifting at 15:00 and pressing at 18:00. Drying therefore starts at 18:00.

questions.prompt: Arrange the work in the invented Harrow Lane weaving shed. Any order that obeys the shed rules counts.
questions.context: Shed rules: spinning needs cleaned fiber. Warping, setting the lengthwise threads, needs spun thread. Weaving needs the warp set. Washing follows weaving. Dyeing is done on washed cloth and needs the dye bath mixed first.
questions.explanation: The main chain is clean, spin, warp, weave, wash, dye. Mixing the dye bath is independent, so it may happen anywhere before dyeing.

questions.prompt: Match each tool in the Harrow Lane glossary to the stage where it is used.
questions.context: Invented glossary. Comb: straightens loose fibers. Spindle: twists fibers into thread. Shuttle: carries weft thread across the warp. Picking tray: sorts seed husks from loose fiber. Heddle frame: lifts alternate warp threads while weaving.
questions.explanation: The comb and picking tray work on loose fiber. The spindle makes thread. The shuttle and heddle frame only make sense once the warp is on the loom.

questions.prompt: Using the inspector's rule card, which stage caused the fault in this bolt of cloth?
questions.context: Invented rule card. Thread thickness varies along a yarn: spinning fault. Warp threads cross unevenly: warping fault. Color blotchy after finishing: dyeing fault. Inspector's findings: thickness varies along a yarn, warp crossings even, color even.
questions.explanation: Only the first rule matches the findings. Even warp crossings rule out warping, and even color rules out dyeing, leaving spinning.

questions.prompt: Arrange the work at the invented Quill Street print shop. Any order that obeys the shop rules counts.
questions.context: Shop rules: lock lines into a frame only after the letters are set. Ink only a locked frame. Press a sheet only after inking. Drying and returning letters to the case both wait until pressing is done, in either order.
questions.explanation: Setting, locking, inking and pressing form a fixed chain. Drying and returning the letters are separate jobs that both follow pressing, so either order is valid.

items.label: Press a sheet onto the type

questions.prompt: At a steady pace, how many seconds did each of the 120 sheets take to press?
questions.context: Invented Quill Street log: frame locked 09:10, inked 09:25, pressing from 09:40 to 11:40 for 120 sheets at a steady pace, letters returned 11:55.
questions.explanation: Pressing lasted two hours, or 7,200 seconds. Dividing by 120 sheets gives 60 seconds each. The other times in the log are not pressing time.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: The mills, sheds, print shop, logs and rules here are invented so every answer can be worked out from the clues given. They do not describe how any real place or community made paper, cloth or printed pages.

title: Living Cultures on the Museum Wall
description: Edit draft museum labels for an invented community, fixing tense, wording and credit, then decide whose voice and which sources should shape each label.

sections.title: Fix the Drafts
sections.description: Choose wording that fits a living community.

sections.title: Choose the Voice
sections.description: Decide who authors and which sources fit.

questions.prompt: Which draft label accurately reflects the Council's statement without calling the community extinct?
questions.context: Invented case: the Marrow Creek Weavers' Council writes in 2026, "We still gather each autumn to weave reed lanterns, and apprentices learn the patterns from our elders."

options.label: The Marrow Creek people wove reed lanterns before disappearing from the region.
Marrow Creek weavers continue to make reed lanterns each autumn, and apprentices learn patterns from elders.
Reed lanterns are a relic of a vanished way of life.
Marrow Creek people once wove reed lanterns, a practice now lost.

questions.explanation: Only draft b matches the community's own present-tense account. The others describe the practice as ended, which the source directly contradicts.

questions.prompt: Which caption best credits the lantern using the object record?
questions.context: Invented object record: reed lantern, made 2024 by weaver Ines Okoro-Vale, a member of the Marrow Creek Weavers' Council, which approved the caption wording.

options.label: Reed lantern, 2024, by Ines Okoro-Vale, Marrow Creek Weavers' Council
Lantern from an ancient culture, museum collection

questions.explanation: The record names the maker, date and community, so a good caption uses them. The others omit known credit or add unsupported, judgmental labels.

questions.prompt: Match each problem phrase in a draft to the edit it needs.
questions.context: Invented case: the Council's 2026 statement says its weavers are active today. Edits: change tense, replace judgmental wording, or remove a claim the source contradicts.

left.label: Weavers were known for their lanterns

questions.explanation: Past tense wrongly implies the practice ended, "primitive" and "crude" are value judgments, and "vanished" contradicts the supplied present-day source.

questions.prompt: Review each draft line against the facts, then choose the right edit.
questions.context: Invented facts: the Council meets monthly, and the 2024 lantern was made by Ines Okoro-Vale, whose name the Council wants shown on the label.

cells.label: "Marrow Creek weavers used to meet monthly."

questions.explanation: The first line is accurate and current. The second wrongly uses past tense, and the third leaves out a maker the record names.

questions.prompt: Which source should author the label text describing how the tradition is practiced today?
questions.context: Invented sources: a 2026 Council statement, an 1890 outside traveler's diary, a museum curator's guess, and a tourism brochure.

options.label: The Marrow Creek Weavers' Council 2026 statement
The curator's guess from similar objects

questions.explanation: Present-day practice is best described by the people who practice it, in their own current words. The other sources are outsiders, dated, or guesses.

questions.prompt: Put these label-making steps in a respectful order.

items.label: Ask the Council which terms and voices to use
Draft the label from the Council's own statement
Send the draft to the Council for correction

questions.explanation: Consultation comes first, drafting draws on the Council's words, the Council reviews the draft, and only then does the label go on the wall.

questions.prompt: Connect each source to every claim it directly supports.
questions.context: Invented sources. Council statement: "We meet monthly and elders teach apprentices." 1890 diary: an outsider reports seeing reed lanterns at a market. Object record: lantern made 2024 by Ines Okoro-Vale.
questions.explanation: Each source supports only what it actually states. The diary shows an outsider's observation in 1890, not current practice or the community's own view.

questions.prompt: How should the label use the 1890 outsider diary responsibly?
questions.context: Invented case: the diary is a genuine primary source from its time, but its author was a visiting outsider writing for a distant audience.

options.label: Treat it as the final word on the community's culture
Cite it as a dated outside observation, not the community's own account
Use it to say the practice ended after 1890
Discard it because it is old

questions.explanation: A primary source can still be biased or incomplete. Separate what it records from interpretation, and keep it distinct from the community's present voice.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: The Marrow Creek community, its Council, people, objects and documents are entirely invented for practice. They do not describe any real community or tradition. The skills apply to real labels, which should rely on community-authored, current sources.

title: Many Hands Made This
description: A joint-solving puzzle set: read three invented clue cards per case, then combine them, match roles, agree on timelines and merge duplicate names to show a tool had many contributors.

sections.title: Shared puzzles
sections.description: Read your card aloud, then solve together.

sections.title: Group timelines
sections.description: Agree on one order before checking.

questions.prompt: Combine the three cards. Who paid for the Pell Quay lantern prototype?
questions.context: Invented case. Four people, Mei, Dev, Rosa and Tomas, each did exactly one job: sketch, wind test, funding, hinge improvement. Card A: Mei ran the wind test; Dev did not draw the sketch. Card B: The funder was not Mei or Rosa. Card C: Dev improved the hinge; Rosa drew the sketch.
questions.explanation: Mei tested, Rosa sketched and Dev improved the hinge, which leaves funding to Tomas. Card B narrows the funder to Dev or Tomas, and Card C rules out Dev.

questions.prompt: Match each contributor to the job their card proves.
questions.context: Invented rain gauge case. Card A: Ana did not fund or improve it; her name is on the daily trial readings. Card B: Ben rebuilt Ana's funnel to reduce splashing. Card C: Chidi's receipt covers the copper tube.
questions.explanation: Ana's readings show testing, Ben's funnel rebuild is the improvement, and Chidi's receipt shows funding. Each job needed a different person.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion do all three cards together support about the Kestrel Street lantern?
questions.context: Invented case. Card A: Ledger, 12 Mar: 40 coins from Lena for lantern glass. Card B: Trial sheet signed by Priya, 15 Mar: wick holder failed twice in wind. Card C: Note by Omar, 20 Mar: fixed holder with a clip.

options.label: Three named people did different jobs, so no one person's work covers every card
Priya's failure report caused Omar's clip

questions.explanation: The cards show distinct work by Lena, Priya and Omar. The cards do not state a cause for the clip, and Lena's payment came first.

questions.prompt: Connect each person to every contribution their cards document. Some people appear more than once.
questions.context: Invented Nimbus kite reel case. Card A: Sana and Jo both signed the line-strength test sheet. Card B: Receipts from Luis and Jo both paid for spools. Card C: The handle redesign is signed by Luis only.
questions.explanation: Five links are documented: Sana and Jo tested, Jo and Luis paid, and Luis redesigned the handle. Several people share jobs, which is typical of team-made tools.

questions.prompt: Agree on one timeline for the Pell Quay lantern. Order the four steps from first to last.
questions.context: Invented case. Card A: The funder paid for the batch that Mei later tested. Card B: Tomas paid only after seeing Rosa's sketch. Card C: Dev based his hinge fix on Mei's test notes.

items.label: Tomas pays for the first batch

questions.explanation: The three cards chain the steps: sketch, funding, test, then improvement. Each card links one step to the next.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for the invented Seed Library catalogue. Any order that obeys all cards is accepted.
questions.context: Invented case. Card A: Quinn tested the labels with visitors only after Nadia had written them. Card B: Quinn's test took place at the cabinet, which Peter had already bought. Card C: Ravi revised the labels using Quinn's visitor notes.
questions.explanation: Writing the labels and buying the cabinet both come before the test, in either order. Revision follows the test.

questions.prompt: Use the card dates to order the invented Marsh Bridge cart steps from earliest to latest.
questions.context: Invented case. Card A: Fatima funded the build on day 4. Card B: Yan's wheel test was 3 days after the funding. Card C: Grace improved the axle 5 days after Yan's test; Hal's sketch was 6 days before the funding.
questions.explanation: Hal's sketch falls on day −2, funding on day 4, the test on day 7 and the axle improvement on day 12.

questions.prompt: Merge matching names across the cards. How many different people contributed to the invented Dune Road bike bell?
questions.context: Invented case. Card A: Ledger entry shows 'W. Hart' paid for the prototypes. Card B: The test log is signed 'Wren Hart', and a note says W. Hart and Wren Hart are the same person. Card C: Ola Pike redesigned the clasp; Jun Reyes drew the sketch.
questions.explanation: W. Hart and Wren Hart are one person, so the contributors are Wren Hart, Ola Pike and Jun Reyes. Checking names across records avoids double counting.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All tools, people, towns and records in this quiz are invented for practice. They are not real history. Players can take turns reading a card aloud and solve together.

title: Letters Across the Border
description: Guide an invented river-crossing family through three delayed letters, read their records, and check the outcome of your branch. You get a separate evidence score out of 3 and two preference scales: wait for proof to move early, and family on its own to neighbor network.

sections.title: Three Letters
sections.description: Choose how the invented family responds.

sections.title: Reading the Records
sections.description: Work from the family's own paperwork.

sections.title: Your Outcome File
sections.description: Check what your branch produced.

dimensions.description: How readily you act before a delayed message is confirmed.
How much you lean on neighbors and community word over the family's own records.

questions.prompt: Letter 1 arrives three weeks late. What does the invented Reyes-Hart family do first?
questions.context: Invented scenario: the Reyes-Hart family runs a wagon shop at a river ford between two made-up districts. Letter 1 says a buyer will pay 40 coins for their spare cart if they confirm before the fair closes.
questions.explanation: This is a taste choice with no correct answer. It adds to your timing and neighbor-network lean, not to your evidence score.

options.label: Wait for a second letter confirming the offer
Ask neighbors who crossed recently whether the buyer is reliable
Sell the cart now to a local dealer
Ask neighbors, and accept the offer if two of them vouch for the buyer

questions.prompt: Letter 2 says the buyer wants proof the cart is sound. How much do you rely on Ines's written note?
questions.context: Invented scenario: Ines is a wheelwright neighbor who offers to inspect the cart and write a note. The family could also inspect and describe it themselves.
questions.explanation: There is no right setting. Leaning toward Ines raises your neighbor-network lean, while leaning toward the family's own inspection lowers it.

questions.prompt: Letter 3 confirms the offer closes at the end of day 31. It is day 22. What do you do?
questions.context: Invented scenario: a neighbor's wagon train leaves today and can carry the reply. The official post-house is closed for four more days. Day 0 is the day Letter 1 was written.
questions.explanation: Both options are reasonable and unscored. Your pick adds to both of your lean results, and it decides which outcome file you check at the end.

options.label: Send the reply now with the neighbor's wagon train
Hold the reply until the post-house reopens

questions.prompt: Which statement is an inference rather than something the letter itself shows?
questions.context: Invented letter excerpt, dated 3 March and stamped received 24 March: "A buyer named Tomas will pay 40 coins for the cart, if the answer reaches him before the fair closes. I suspect he is short of cash."
questions.explanation: The dates, the reported offer, and the condition appear in the record. The writer's suspicion about the buyer's money is an interpretation, not evidence the record shows.

options.label: The letter carries a 3 March date and a 24 March received stamp
The writer reports an offer of 40 coins for the cart
The buyer is short of cash
The offer depends on the answer arriving before the fair closes

questions.prompt: Using the post-house notes, put the steps of the first letter's journey in the order they happened.
questions.context: Invented notes: the carter left 6 days after the letter was written. Mara's reply was written 1 day after delivery. The river crossing happened 10 days after the carter left, and delivery came 5 days after the crossing.
questions.explanation: Counting from day 0: carter day 6, crossing day 16, delivery day 21, reply day 22. Those offsets give a single order.

questions.prompt: Rank these record-keeping habits from the one you would start first to the one you would start last.
questions.context: Imagine adding one habit at a time to the family's chest of records.
questions.explanation: This is a preference ranking with no correct order. It feeds your two preference scales, not your evidence score.

items.label: Dated copies of every letter we send
A list of neighbors who can vouch for people and carry word
A cash reserve for sudden decisions
A shared notebook of neighbors' news for early tips

questions.prompt: Did the reply reach the brother before the offer closed, and by how many days?
questions.context: Invented outcome file: the wagon train reached the river on day 25 and waited 2 days for the water to fall. It crossed that day, and the reply was delivered 3 days after crossing. The offer closed at the end of day 31.
questions.explanation: The train crossed on day 27 after waiting, and delivery came on day 30. That is one day before the offer closed. This is a fictional result, not a verdict on your choice.

questions.prompt: On what day did the reply reach the brother, and how does that compare with the offer's closing?
questions.context: Invented outcome file: the post-house reopened on day 26. The official post took 6 days to the border post, then a 2-day customs hold, then 3 days to the brother's town. The offer closed at the end of day 31.
questions.explanation: Starting day 26, adding 6, 2, and 3 gives day 37. That is six days after the offer closed. This is a fictional result, not a verdict on your choice.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: The family, districts, letters, ledgers, and outcomes are invented for this quiz and do not depict any real community. Your evidence score (out of 3) and your two decision-lean scales are kept separate. Taste choices are never marked right or wrong.

title: The Map Was Updated
description: Tap symbols on schematic invented maps, compare old and new legends, and put map editions in order to work out what changed and when.

sections.title: Tap the clue
sections.description: Four invented map sheets

sections.title: Read the legend
sections.description: Legends and ink codes

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All maps, places, dates and legends here are invented schematic diagrams, not real surveys. Each task lists every legend and rule you need. Every hotspot is described in words, so the quiz can be played without seeing the diagram.

questions.prompt: Tap the symbol showing a railway that was added after the original survey.
questions.context: Invented sheet of Marlow Vale. Legend: black ink = 1891 survey; red ink = added at the 1896 revision. Double line = road; line with cross ticks = railway; wavy line = stream.
questions.explanation: Railways use cross ticks, and red ink marks 1896 additions. The black-ink railway was already in the original survey, so only the red one qualifies.

diagram.title: Marlow Vale sheet, surveyed 1891, revised 1896 (invented)
diagram.description: Four marked features in a grid. Top-left: black double line, a road. Top-right: red line with cross ticks, a railway. Bottom-left: black line with cross ticks, a railway. Bottom-right: wavy blue line, a stream.

questions.prompt: Tap the symbol for a building that was already gone by the 1904 revision.
questions.context: Invented sheet of Pell Cross, surveyed 1888. Legend: solid black square = building standing in 1888; dotted outline = building removed by 1904; solid red square = building added by 1904.
questions.explanation: A dotted outline means the building existed in 1888 but had been removed by 1904. Solid black squares still stood, and the red square is a new addition.

diagram.title: Pell Cross sheet, surveyed 1888, revised 1904 (invented)
diagram.description: Four building symbols. Top-left: solid black square labelled Chapel. Top-right: dotted outline square labelled Granary. Bottom-left: solid red square labelled School. Bottom-right: solid black square with a flag labelled Customs shed.

questions.prompt: Tap the mill that stands upstream of the ferry, on the west bank.
questions.context: Invented Tarn River sheet. North is at the top. The river flows from the bottom edge toward the sea at the top edge. The ferry marker sits at the sheet's centre.
questions.explanation: Water flows toward the top, so upstream is toward the bottom. West is the left bank. The lower-left mill meets both conditions.

diagram.title: Tarn River ferry crossing (invented)
diagram.description: A river runs vertically down the middle of the sheet, flowing upward toward the sea. A ferry marker sits at the centre. Four mills: one in each corner area, two on the left (west) bank and two on the right (east) bank, one above and one below the ferry on each side.

questions.prompt: Tap the margin element that was added by hand after the 1899 printing, not by the printed survey.
questions.context: Invented printed sheet titled Revised 1899. Printed elements come from the publisher. Handwriting was added later by an unknown owner.
questions.explanation: Printed margin items belong to the 1899 sheet. The pencil note is a later addition by someone else, so it is a separate piece of evidence to question.

diagram.title: Margin of a sheet printed in 1899 (invented)
diagram.description: Top-left: printed title box reading Revised 1899. Middle-right: printed compass rose. Bottom-left: printed scale bar. Bottom-right: pencil handwriting reading Bridge fell 1907.

questions.prompt: Which change from the 1892 legend to the 1901 legend shows a feature type that had no symbol before?
questions.context: 1892 legend: open square = school; cross = church; thin dashes = footpath. 1901 legend: open square = school; cross = church (label in bolder type); thin dashes = footpath, drawn lighter; dashes with ticks = tramway; legend box moved to the right margin.
questions.explanation: Only the tramway symbol is a new entry. Moving the box, bolder lettering and lighter lines change appearance but describe feature types the 1892 map already had.

options.label: The legend box moved to the right margin
A tramway symbol of dashes with ticks was added
The church label was printed in bolder type
The footpath dashes were drawn lighter

questions.prompt: Fen Meadow changed symbols between editions. Which legend change best supports the idea that the marsh was reclaimed?
questions.context: 1890 legend: blue dashes = marsh; ring symbols = woodland. 1906 legend: ring symbols = woodland; green dots = pasture. No blue-dash marsh appears anywhere on the 1906 sheet.
questions.explanation: Pasture appears and marsh vanishes from both legend and sheet, which supports reclamation as an inference. The map shows the change but not who did it or why.

options.label: Pasture symbol added and marsh symbol dropped
The legend title was reprinted in capitals
Both marsh and woodland symbols were kept

questions.prompt: Match each marked feature to what its ink or line style tells you about the edition history.
questions.context: Invented sheet. Black ink = original 1890 survey. Red ink = added at the 1898 revision. Dotted black outline = removed by 1898. Pencil = added later by an unknown hand, undated.
questions.explanation: Ink and line style carry the dating clues: red means 1898 addition, dotted means removed, black means original, and pencil gives no reliable date.

questions.prompt: Put the four sheets in order from earliest to latest edition.
questions.context: Invented town. Once a feature is drawn it stays on later sheets until removed. The ferry ran only until the bridge opened. A tram line was added only after the bridge was complete. Sheet P: bridge piers with ferry still shown. Sheet Q: finished bridge, no ferry, no tram. Sheet R: ferry, no bridge. Sheet S: bridge and tram.
questions.explanation: R has no bridge, P shows it under construction, Q shows it open with the ferry gone, and S adds the tram that required a finished bridge.

title: Soundscapes of Everyday Life
description: Play four short original sound cues from invented office devices, decode each with a supplied legend, then sort four dated archive cards and judge what records can prove.

sections.title: Listen and decode
sections.description: Four original clips with a device legend

sections.title: Archive cards
sections.description: Dated records and source reasoning

questions.prompt: Play the clip. Using the legend, which sequence of mechanical actions does it demonstrate?
questions.context: Legend for the invented Desk Writer: low 300 Hz pulse = key strike; high 880 Hz ping = line-end bell; long low 260 Hz tone = carriage return slide.
questions.transcript: Three short low pulses at 300 Hz, evenly spaced; then one bright 880 Hz ping; then one long low 260 Hz tone.

options.label: Keys, then bell, then carriage return
Bell, then keys, then carriage return
Keys, then carriage return, then bell
Carriage return, then keys, then bell

questions.explanation: The legend maps three 300 Hz pulses to key strikes, the 880 Hz ping to the bell, and the final long low tone to the carriage return.

questions.prompt: Play the clip. Which number was dialed on this invented rotary desk phone?
questions.context: Legend: each short 600 Hz tick = one dial pulse. A digit equals the pulses before a pause longer than 0.5 seconds. The long 300 Hz tone means the dial returned to rest.
questions.transcript: Three quick 600 Hz ticks, a pause of about 0.6 seconds, four quick 600 Hz ticks, another short pause, then one long 300 Hz tone.
questions.explanation: Three pulses, a gap over half a second, then four pulses give digits 3 and 4. The final long tone is only the dial returning to rest.

questions.prompt: Play the clip. How many date-wheel steps occur before the stamp press?
questions.context: Legend for an invented hand date stamp: each 450 Hz tick = one date-wheel step; the low 200 Hz thump = the stamp press.
questions.transcript: Three evenly spaced 450 Hz ticks, a gap, one low 200 Hz thump, then a single 450 Hz tick afterward.
questions.explanation: Only ticks before the 200 Hz thump count. The final tick comes after the press, so it belongs to the next setting, not this one.

questions.prompt: Play the clip. Which filing-cabinet action occurs exactly twice?
questions.context: Legend for an invented cabinet: long 350 Hz tone = drawer slide; short 650 Hz tick = folder flip; short low 250 Hz thump = drawer closing.
questions.transcript: One long 350 Hz tone; two short 650 Hz ticks spaced a quarter second apart; then one short low 250 Hz thump.
questions.explanation: The 650 Hz tick appears twice, so two folders were flipped. The slide and the closing thump each occur once.

questions.prompt: Order these documented first uses from earliest to latest, using the dates on the cards.
questions.context: Invented dossier from the Larkmere Freight Office. Cards record first documented use in this office only, not invention or wider adoption. Typed invoices: 2 Nov 1908. Date stamp on mail log: 14 May 1921. Dial desk phone: 30 Jan 1934. Filing cabinet order: 6 Jun 1915.
questions.explanation: Sorting the supplied dates gives 1908, 1915, 1921, 1934. The cards document this office's first uses, so they say nothing about other offices.

questions.prompt: Using only these clerk notes, order the four purchases from first to last.
questions.context: Invented notes from Harbor Dairy Cooperative: the typewriter was rented before the date stamp was bought. The stamp was bought before the cabinet arrived. The cabinet arrived before the dial phone was installed.
questions.explanation: The three notes chain together: typewriter, stamp, cabinet, phone. Each note gives a before-and-after link, so no extra dates are needed.

questions.prompt: An undated tape contains a typewriter bell. What can an archivist safely conclude from the sound alone?
questions.context: Invented case: a Larkmere cassette has no label or log, and the bell sound is clear. Typewriter-style bells were present in many places and for many years.

options.label: It was recorded in the office's first typing year
The sound alone cannot date it; a dated log or label is needed
It proves the speaker worked as a clerk
It proves the building had no telephones

questions.explanation: A sound shows what was audible, not when. Dating requires documented evidence, and separating what a record shows from inference is core source analysis.

questions.prompt: Which item is best treated as a primary source about the freight office's 1908 work?
questions.context: Invented items: (1) the office's own typed 1908 invoice; (2) a 1990 magazine summary of its history; (3) a student timeline built from both; (4) a museum label written last year.
questions.explanation: The invoice was created as part of the office's own work. Later summaries interpret it, and even a primary source can be biased or incomplete.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All sounds are original synthesized tones, not recordings of real machines, and each question has a text transcript. The devices, offices and dates are invented for practice and do not describe real adoption history.

title: The Cropped Photograph
description: Study an invented street scene twice: first as a tight crop, then as the full frame. Decide which claims each view supports, weakens, or leaves open.

sections.title: Read the crop
sections.description: Work only from what the cropped view shows.

sections.title: Reveal the full frame
sections.description: Revise claims once more of the scene is visible.

questions.prompt: Which zone in the crop gives the most direct visible evidence of the hour?
questions.context: Invented teaching scene, not a real photograph. The crop shows a tower clock, a shuttered shop door, an unlit street lamp, and an empty pavement strip.
questions.explanation: A clock face is a visible record of time. The shutter, lamp and pavement may invite guesses, but none of them states the hour directly.

diagram.title: Crop of an invented street scene
diagram.description: Schematic rectangles for the cropped frame: tower clock at top left, shuttered door in the middle, lamp at right, pavement strip along the bottom.

zones.label: Tower clock face reading ten past four

questions.prompt: Which claim does the cropped view itself support?
questions.context: Invented crop: a stretch of pavement with no people in view, a bakery shutter pulled down, and a clock reading ten past four. No caption is supplied.
questions.explanation: A crop can only show what sits inside its edges. It supports a statement about this segment at this moment, not about the whole town or anyone's motives.

options.label: No people are visible on this street segment at ten past four.
Every shop in town was closed that afternoon.
Residents were deliberately avoiding the area.
Police had cleared the street of pedestrians.

questions.prompt: Sort each statement by whether the crop shows it or whether it goes beyond the crop.
questions.context: Same invented crop: empty pavement, bakery shutter down, tower clock at ten past four.
questions.explanation: Shutter and clock are visible details. Motives and all-afternoon claims are interpretations that need evidence beyond a single moment in a cropped frame.

left.label: A shutter is down over the bakery door
The tower clock reads ten past four
The street stayed empty all afternoon

questions.prompt: Put these archive-reading steps in a sensible order, from first to last.
questions.explanation: Good source analysis starts with observing, then reflecting, then questioning, and only then checks other records so inferences are tested rather than assumed.

items.label: Note what is visibly in the frame
Reflect on what those details might suggest
Ask what is missing from the frame
Compare your ideas with other records

questions.prompt: Which zone, outside what the crop included, shows people present at the event?
questions.context: Invented full-frame diagram, left to right. The far left is the crop's area. The rest shows the plaza beyond the street's edge.
questions.explanation: The crowd zone adds direct visual evidence of people nearby. The banner and empty stand name or equip the event but do not show attendance, and the crop area is unchanged.

diagram.title: Full frame of the invented scene
diagram.description: Schematic rectangles: crop area at far left, plaza zone in the centre, banner pole at upper right, reviewing stand at lower right.

questions.prompt: The crop's caption said the whole town stayed home. Which revised caption does the full frame support?
questions.context: Full frame (invented): the cropped street is empty, while a crowd stands in the plaza just past its edge under a Closing Day banner.
questions.explanation: The best caption keeps the true detail, an empty segment, and adds the crowd. The others overstate crowd size, invent a cancellation, or assign opinions the frame cannot show.

options.label: One street segment was empty while a crowd gathered just beyond it.
A huge crowd packed every street in town.
The Closing Day event was cancelled.
The crowd approved of the shop closures.

questions.prompt: For each claim, decide what the full frame does to it.
questions.context: Full frame (invented): empty cropped segment, clock at ten past four, shuttered shop row, and a crowd in the adjoining plaza. No interviews or captions are supplied.
questions.explanation: The segment stayed empty, the crowd is visible, and the plaza is not empty. Why shop owners closed cannot be read from shutters alone, so that claim stays open.

cells.label: No one stood on the cropped segment at ten past four.
The plaza was as empty as the cropped street.
Shop owners closed to avoid the event.
Many people were nearby around ten past four.

questions.prompt: Link each claim to the full-frame details that directly show it. Some claims need two.
questions.context: Invented details: the clock shows ten past four in both views; the plaza holds a crowd; shutters are down on the shop row; a banner names Closing Day.
questions.explanation: Activity is shown by the crowd plus the banner naming the event. The clock fixes the moment, and the shutters directly show closed shop fronts. No detail shows motive.

left.label: A named event was underway in the scene
The photo shows one specific moment

right.label: Shutters down on the shop row

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: The street, crowd, banner and clock are an invented teaching scene drawn as simple schematic diagrams. They are not real photographs or historical evidence. Only the source-analysis ideas come from real reference guides.

title: Footnote Treasure Hunt
description: Follow invented source cards through eight local-history decisions: pick the card that supports each claim, order footnote trails back to primary records, and sort cards by type.

questions.prompt: A brochure says Alderbrook opened the first public library in its county, citing only an 1894 opening date. Which card would establish the comparison?
questions.context: Invented scenario. Alderbrook and its county are made up for this quiz.
questions.explanation: Firstness is a comparison. You need opening dates for every library in the county, not just Alderbrook's date or someone's confident memory.

options.label: Alderbrook library board minutes recording its 1894 opening
A county register listing every public library with its opening date
A 1950 memoir saying locals always knew Alderbrook was first
Insufficient evidence: no card type could establish this

questions.prompt: Claim: the 1912 Harlow Mill strike lasted nine days. Which card supports the length of the strike?
questions.context: Invented scenario. The mill and strike are made up. Strike days are days with no wages earned.
questions.explanation: The payroll book shows both ends: wages stop on 3 March and resume on 12 March, so nine days. The diary gives only a start, and the retrospective is vague.

options.label: Owner's diary: 'Pickets at the gate this morning,' dated 3 March
Payroll book: no wages 3 to 11 March; wages resume 12 March
1960 newspaper retrospective: 'about a week and a half'
Insufficient evidence: no card helps with duration

questions.prompt: Claim: Verity Academy was the first school in the region to admit girls. Which card supports that claim?
questions.context: Invented scenario. The academy and region are made up. Cards: a 1921 prospectus, an obituary, a classroom photo caption.
questions.explanation: Every card concerns only Verity Academy. None gives admission dates for other schools, so the claim of being first stays unsupported.

options.label: The 1921 prospectus announcing that girls enroll from autumn
A teacher's obituary calling the school 'pioneering'
A 1921 photo caption describing a mixed class
Insufficient evidence: none of these cards compares other schools' admission dates

questions.prompt: Claim: Rosa Delgado operated the Bell Creek ferry in 1888. Which card most directly supports naming her?
questions.context: Invented scenario. The 1888 directory lists two residents named R. Delgado. The ferry licence says only 'R. Delgado'.
questions.explanation: The licence initial fits two people, and a family tale is later and unchecked. The tax ledger names Rosa and her occupation in the same year.

options.label: 1888 tax ledger entry: 'Rosa Delgado, ferry operator'
A descendant's family story about a ferrywoman
Insufficient evidence: no card names her

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order for tracing a brochure claim to its primary record.
questions.context: Each step needs what the previous step produces: a claim leads to a note number, then a bibliography entry, then an archive box, then the document.
questions.explanation: You must find the note before the bibliography entry, the entry before requesting the box, and the box before checking the document inside against the claim.

items.label: Look up that note in the bibliography
Check the document inside against the claim
Request the archive box named in the entry
Find the note number attached to the claim

questions.prompt: Order the steps for checking a quotation. Any order that respects what each step needs is accepted.
questions.context: You must open the cited page before comparing wording or noticing what it quotes. Reading an earlier letter's catalog entry requires first noticing that the page quotes it.
questions.explanation: Both comparing wording and spotting the quoted letter need the page open. The catalog entry follows spotting the letter, but the wording comparison can happen before or after.

items.label: Notice the page is quoting an earlier letter
Compare the page's wording with the quotation
Find the letter's manuscript catalog entry
Note the quotation and its footnote
Open the cited edition to the cited page

questions.prompt: A map caption and the town history give different founding dates. Order a fair way to resolve the conflict.
questions.context: Both need their citations listed first. Each record must be fetched before the final statement. The two fetches may happen in either order.
questions.explanation: Spotting the conflict starts the work, and listing both citations comes next. Each underlying record is fetched, in either order, before you state which date the records support.

items.label: State which date the records support
Fetch the record behind the map caption
Fetch the record behind the history's date
List the citation given for each date

questions.prompt: Match each invented archive card to what it is, judging only from the description given.
questions.context: Primary records were created as part of people's lives. Secondary accounts are written later about events. If a card lacks a stated origin, its type is unclear.
questions.explanation: Receipts and diaries arise from events themselves, though they can still be biased. A later textbook interprets them, and an undated, unsigned note leaves its origin unclear.

left.label: Ferry toll receipt signed on the day of the crossing
1975 textbook chapter summarizing the ferry era
Passenger's diary entry written during the trip
Undated, unsigned note with no stated origin

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All towns, schools, mills, ferries and archive cards here are invented for practice. Answers follow only the evidence stated in each case, not real local history.

title: One Claim, Five Echoes
description: Five invented posts repeat one harmless claim about a museum cafe. Trace who cited whom, follow each chain to its root, order the times and judge what the log really establishes.

questions.prompt: Match each post to the role it plays in the log. Several posts can share one role.
questions.context: Invented log. Obs 1 is Ines's call to the museum's recorded phone message at 08:50, which says the cafe opens at 9:00 on Saturdays. Obs 2 is Pia's photo of the door sign, taken on site at 10:20, showing 9:00 on Saturdays. Posts: Post 1, Ines, 09:10: "I called the museum and the recorded message says the cafe opens at 9:00 on Saturdays." Post 2, Kofi, 09:25: "Ines posted this, so the cafe opens at 9:00 on Saturdays." Post 3, Lena, 10:05: "Kofi's post says the cafe opens at 9:00 on Saturdays." Post 4, Mo, 10:40: "Pia's door-sign photo shows 9:00 on Saturdays, and Kofi's post agrees." Post 5, Nell, 11:15: "Lena's post says 9:00 on Saturdays. I have not read Ines's or Mo's posts." One role on the right fits none of the posts.

right.label: Only repeats one earlier post, with nothing else
Combines an observation with a repeated post

questions.explanation: Post 1 relays Ines's own call. Posts 2, 3 and 5 each name one earlier post and nothing else. Post 4 names the door-sign photo and also repeats Post 2. No post corrects another.

questions.prompt: Connect each post to every source it directly names, without following the chain further back.
questions.context: Invented log. Obs 1 is Ines's call to the museum's recorded phone message at 08:50, which says the cafe opens at 9:00 on Saturdays. Obs 2 is Pia's photo of the door sign, taken on site at 10:20, showing 9:00 on Saturdays. Post 1, Ines, 09:10: "I called the museum and the recorded message says the cafe opens at 9:00 on Saturdays." Post 2, Kofi, 09:25: "Ines posted this, so the cafe opens at 9:00 on Saturdays." Post 3, Lena, 10:05: "Kofi's post says the cafe opens at 9:00 on Saturdays." Post 4, Mo, 10:40: "Pia's door-sign photo shows 9:00 on Saturdays, and Kofi's post agrees." Post 5, Nell, 11:15: "Lena's post says 9:00 on Saturdays. I have not read Ines's or Mo's posts." A link means the post itself names that source. Do not add links for sources further back in a chain.
questions.explanation: Post 1 names the phone message, Post 2 names Post 1, Post 3 names Post 2 and Post 5 names Post 3. Post 4 names two sources, the door-sign photo and Post 2. Nell's remark about not reading other posts adds no link.

questions.prompt: Connect each post to every independent observation at the end of its chain of citations.
questions.context: Invented log. Obs 1 is Ines's call to the museum's recorded phone message at 08:50. Obs 2 is Pia's photo of the door sign, taken on site at 10:20. Direct citations: Post 1 names Obs 1. Post 2 names Post 1. Post 3 names Post 2. Post 4 names Obs 2 and Post 2. Post 5 names Post 3. A root is an observation you reach by following citations back until a post names an observation instead of another post. Link a post to every root it reaches, however many posts lie in between.
questions.explanation: Posts 1, 2, 3 and 5 all lead back to the phone message alone. Post 4 reaches the door-sign photo directly and the phone message by way of Post 2, so it has two roots.

questions.prompt: Put these seven log entries in the order they happened, earliest first.
questions.context: Times in the invented log: Post 3 at 10:05; door-sign photo taken at 10:20; Post 1 at 09:10; phone message call at 08:50; Post 5 at 11:15; Post 2 at 09:25; Post 4 at 10:40. Posts show the time they were published.
questions.explanation: The call at 08:50 comes first, then Posts 1, 2 and 3 at 09:10, 09:25 and 10:05. The photo is taken at 10:20, after Post 3 and before Post 4, which names it. Post 5 closes at 11:15.

questions.prompt: How many independent observations does this log contain?
questions.context: Invented log. Observations made first-hand: Ines's call to the recorded phone message (Obs 1) and Pia's photo of the door sign (Obs 2). Direct citations: Post 1 names Obs 1. Post 2 names Post 1. Post 3 names Post 2. Post 4 names Obs 2 and Post 2. Post 5 names Post 3. Count independent roots, not posts.

options.label: Seven, counting posts and observations together

questions.explanation: Only the phone message and the door-sign photo were directly heard or seen. The five posts spread those two observations, so more posts do not mean more independent evidence.

questions.prompt: Post 3 was published at 10:05. What does it add beyond what Post 2 already offered?
questions.context: Invented log. Post 2 (Kofi, 09:25) names Post 1, which names the phone message call (Obs 1). Post 3 (Lena, 10:05) names only Post 2. Pia's door-sign photo (Obs 2) was taken at 10:20.

options.label: Nothing new as evidence: it repeats Post 2, which traces back to Obs 1
Support from the door-sign photo, since the photo was taken that morning

questions.explanation: Post 3 names only Post 2, so it carries the same single root. The photo did not yet exist at 10:05 and Post 3 does not name it in any case.

questions.prompt: Suppose Obs 1 turns out to be an out-of-date recording. Which posts are left with no root at all?
questions.context: Invented log. Roots: Posts 1, 2, 3 and 5 each trace back only to Obs 1, the phone message call. Post 4 traces back to Obs 1 through Post 2 and also directly to Obs 2, the door-sign photo. Rule: a post loses its root support only when every root it reaches has been set aside.

options.label: Posts 1, 2, 3 and 5; Post 4 still rests on Obs 2

questions.explanation: Setting aside Obs 1 removes the only root of Posts 1, 2, 3 and 5. Post 4 keeps the door-sign photo, so one root remains.

questions.prompt: Judge each statement against the log.
questions.context: Invented log. Obs 1 (phone message call, 08:50) and Obs 2 (door-sign photo, 10:20) are the only observations. Citations: Post 1 names Obs 1; Post 2 names Post 1; Post 3 names Post 2; Post 4 names Obs 2 and Post 2; Post 5 names Post 3. Times: Post 1 09:10, Post 2 09:25, Post 3 10:05, Post 4 10:40, Post 5 11:15. The log shows who reported what and when. No one in the log saw the cafe actually open on a Saturday.

cells.label: Five separate people each checked the opening time themselves.
Post 5 and Post 1 trace back to the same root.
Post 3 was published before the door-sign photo was taken.
The log establishes that the cafe actually opens at 9:00 on Saturdays, not merely that 9:00 was reported or posted.

questions.explanation: Only Ines and Pia made observations, so five separate checks are not shown. Post 4 reaches Obs 2 and Obs 1, and Posts 1 and 5 share Obs 1. Post 3 at 10:05 precedes the 10:20 photo. The log records a phone message and a photo of posted hours, and no one saw the cafe actually open, so it does not establish the real opening time.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz invented posts, observations and toy rules
NAMLE: Key Questions for Analyzing Media (supports asking about sources and evidence; not a single right reading)

note: The museum cafe, posts, people and observations are invented, and no real news is involved. Each answer follows the toy rules stated in its task. The reference supports the habit of asking where a claim comes from and what evidence stands behind it; it does not give one correct reading of any real post and does not show that this quiz improves media skills.

title: Objects After Dark: Irish Halloween
description: A carved turnip, a mask, a needle and a bowl of clay each carried a different story. Explore specific Irish customs recorded by the National Museum of Ireland.

questions.prompt: Before the familiar pumpkin lantern, which vegetable does the National Museum of Ireland describe people carving into scary lanterns?
questions.explanation: The museum describes carved turnips carried or set on windowsills, and presents the pumpkin version as an American development. This is a recorded regional practice, not one universal origin story.

questions.prompt: In the museum's account of guising, what did visitors offer a household in exchange for a treat?
questions.explanation: Guisers performed for households. The exchange helps explain why a treat visit could involve an actual ‘trick’ or performance, rather than simply collecting food.

questions.prompt: Match each object to the practice recorded in the museum's account.
questions.explanation: The materials had different places in the customs: crosses hung for protection and luck, masks worn to frighten, and metal objects carried by some travellers as protection. These are recorded beliefs and practices, not proof of protective powers.

left.label: Steel needle carried on a journey

right.label: Carried because of fears of spirit abduction
Hung for protection and luck over the coming winter

questions.prompt: In the recorded four-bowl fortune game, what did each bowl symbolise?
questions.explanation: These associations describe a historical fortune-telling game. Selecting an object does not predict anyone's future.
questions.context: The museum describes a blindfolded selection among bowls containing water, a ring, clay and food.

questions.prompt: Why might a spade head or a spinning-wheel part appear under a pillow in the museum's Halloween account?
questions.explanation: The museum records a marriage-divination belief involving several household objects. The surprising object makes sense inside that belief, without making the belief a factual prediction.

options.label: To bring the household prosperity through a harvest ritual
To invite a dream visit from a departed relative
In the belief that it could prompt a dream of a future spouse

questions.prompt: What practical message did the museum associate with stories of the púca spoiling wild fruit after Halloween?
questions.explanation: The museum interprets the púca story as a way to discourage eating damaged fruit after the date. It is a recorded story and its social purpose, not modern food-safety guidance.

options.label: Discouraging children from eating the damaged berries and apples after that date
Explaining how birds carry seeds between orchards
Predicting which trees would blossom first in spring

questions.prompt: The museum compares older summer bonfires in western Ireland with growing Halloween bonfire traditions. What does that comparison help us notice?
questions.explanation: The account distinguishes regions and describes change. Treating a living tradition as one timeless, identical national script would erase that detail.

options.label: Every Irish region always celebrated in an identical way
Traditions can differ by region and change over time
The account proves Halloween bonfires replaced all other fires

questions.prompt: Which dish on the museum’s Halloween food list is mashed potato with cabbage and onions?
questions.explanation: The museum describes colcannon as mashed potato with cabbage and onions, alongside boxty (potato cakes) and báirín breac (cake). A seasonal celebration included a meal, not only sweets.

sources.label: National Museum of Ireland: Halloween traditions, objects and recorded beliefs

note: A source-based look at recorded Irish customs, with regional and historical limits. Supernatural and fortune-telling beliefs are described as beliefs. No copied museum images or instructions to recreate risky practices.

title: Sleepy Hollow: The Chase and the Wink
description: Enter Irving’s ghost tale through eight short retold fragments. Follow a hungry schoolmaster, a jealous rival and a midnight chase—then discover why the ending keeps two explanations alive.

questions.prompt: What tension in Ichabod’s character makes this opening more interesting than a simple portrait of a wise teacher?
questions.explanation: The opening lets reputation and judgment pull apart: learning gives Ichabod social standing without protecting him from credulity. This is a character reading of Irving’s fiction.
questions.context: Original paraphrase of Irving’s fiction. Ichabod Crane teaches the children of Sleepy Hollow and earns extra money giving singing lessons. His neighbours treat him as learned. He eagerly reads accounts of witchcraft, exchanges ghost tales beside warm fires, and walks home alarmed by the sounds outside.

options.label: His neighbours admire his learning, but he readily accepts frightening stories
His neighbours distrust his reading, but he refuses to believe any local story
He secretly dislikes teaching and never speaks outside the school

questions.prompt: Which reading of Ichabod’s courtship best accounts for the future he imagines?
questions.explanation: He imagines both marriage and converting the estate into a different future. The passage supports mixed desire, not either pure romance or complete indifference to Katrina.
questions.context: Original paraphrase. Katrina Van Tassel is the farmer’s only child. Ichabod admires her, then surveys the abundant animals, fields and household comforts. In his imagination the animals become meals, the property becomes money, and he and Katrina travel west with their future family.

options.label: He mainly wants to preserve the Van Tassel farm exactly as it is
He wants Katrina to give up the inheritance before marrying him
His attraction to Katrina is entangled with appetite and material ambition

questions.prompt: Why does the dance make the coming rivalry more than an abstract competition between two suitors?
questions.explanation: The scene puts Ichabod’s hopeful performance beside Brom’s jealousy. It raises the stakes of the rivalry without turning a dance into a promise of marriage.
questions.context: Original paraphrase. At the Van Tassel gathering, Ichabod dances energetically with Katrina, who smiles at him. Brom Bones, the confident horseman who also courts her, sits apart in jealous silence. Later, the guests trade tales of war and the Headless Horseman.

options.label: Katrina’s smile settles which suitor she will eventually marry
Ichabod receives visible encouragement while Brom has to watch
Brom’s silence shows he has withdrawn from the rivalry

questions.prompt: The narration leaves a door closed. How far can you carry each conclusion about the private conversation?
questions.explanation: Ichabod’s changed manner supports disappointment. The narrator supplies no exact dialogue or promise, so the specific cause remains an inference rather than a transcript.
questions.context: Original paraphrase. Ichabod stays after the party to speak privately with Katrina. The narrator admits he does not know what they said. Ichabod soon emerges dejected and rides away, paying no attention to the wealth that delighted him earlier.

cells.label: The meeting appears to have disappointed Ichabod

options.label: An exact statement spoken by Katrina

cells.label: Katrina explicitly promised to marry Brom during that conversation

options.label: Possible, but not established by this telling
Impossible because Ichabod danced with her

questions.prompt: What does this sequence do to the next frightening thing Ichabod sees?
questions.explanation: Earlier mistakes make the reader cautious about Ichabod’s perceptions. They explain his fear and create doubt, but do not logically identify the rider who appears next.
questions.context: Original paraphrase. On the dark road, a whistle seems to answer Ichabod, until he recognises wind in the branches. A pale shape on a tree resolves into exposed wood, and a groan into rubbing boughs. Farther on, a large silent figure beside the brook begins to move.

options.label: It establishes that the next figure must also be a tree
It makes his fear impossible to understand
It gives readers reason to question his first interpretation without settling the next encounter

questions.prompt: Match each detail of the chase to its particular effect on Ichabod’s predicament.
questions.explanation: The saddle adds a mundane loss to supernatural terror; the bridge offers reassurance borrowed from a tale; the hurled object defeats that reassurance. These functions differ even though all occur in one chase.
questions.context: Original paraphrase. The silent rider keeps pace when Ichabod speeds up and slows down. Against the sky, the rider seems headless, with a head on the saddle. Ichabod flees; his own saddle falls and is trampled. He remembers Brom’s tale of a ghost vanishing at the church bridge and rushes across. Looking back for that disappearance, he instead sees the rider hurl the supposed head. It knocks him down.

left.label: The borrowed saddle falls under the pursuer’s hooves
The church bridge comes into view
The rider throws the apparent head

right.label: Turns an expected escape into a final blow
Adds a practical worry about damaged borrowed equipment
Offers a hoped-for boundary to the pursuit

questions.prompt: Which ending preserves what these details allow the reader to suspect without pretending the mystery is solved?
questions.explanation: The pumpkin, rivalry and knowing laughter invite a human-prank reading. A later report offers an ordinary future for Ichabod. Neither is a witnessed confession or proof of a supernatural event.
questions.context: Original paraphrase. The next day, searchers find Ichabod’s hat and a broken pumpkin, but no body. Years later a farmer reports that Ichabod lived elsewhere and entered the law. Brom marries Katrina and laughs knowingly whenever the pumpkin is mentioned. Some local tellers continue to insist that a ghost took the schoolmaster.

options.label: Brom is a plausible prankster behind the chase, but the telling does not conclusively identify the rider
The recovered hat proves that a ghost carried Ichabod away
The farmer’s later report establishes that Brom confessed

questions.prompt: What does the postscript change about how we receive the tale?
questions.explanation: The final frame exposes an entertainer behind the account. Readers can enjoy the scare while recognising that the teller is shaping an audience’s response; the postscript offers a wink, not a definitive culprit.
questions.context: Original paraphrase. A postscript says the account was heard from an entertaining older man at a meeting. When a listener asks what the story proves, the teller offers an absurd chain of reasoning about rejection leading to career success. Pressed about the tale’s extravagance, he admits that he doubts much of his own story.

options.label: It delivers a serious lesson that romantic rejection guarantees success
It makes the performance of storytelling part of the mystery
It turns the entertaining speaker into a reliable eyewitness to the chase

sources.label: Washington Irving: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, complete public-domain text at Project Gutenberg

note: All fragments are original paraphrases of Irving’s public-domain fiction, supplied here so no prior reading is needed. This is the schoolmaster’s story, not a film detective adaptation. Events belong to the telling; neither a real ghost nor Brom’s identity as the rider is proved.

title: The Strange Little Halloween Postcard Gallery
description: Follow a curator’s trail through early Halloween postcards: a fruit automobile, mirror fortune, harvest-field scenes, a personal greeting, and the cards’ later life. Use the museum’s descriptions to infer what each little story does.

sources.label: The Henry Ford object record: Hallowe’en Precautions, circa 1910 (2020.36.1)
The Henry Ford object record: Hallowe’en Postcard, 1907–1908 (2006.36.1)
The Henry Ford object record: Halloween Postcard, circa 1912 (2008.84.1)
The Henry Ford object record: Pumpkin-head Children Bobbing for Apples, 1910–1915 (2018.32.1)
The Henry Ford object record: The Halloween Lantern, 1914 (2007.69.1)
The Henry Ford object record: ‘Hallo e’en. Sh! Ghosts!’ 1909 (94.81.1)
The Henry Ford object record: ‘Curioser and Curioser Allhallowe’en Hallowe’en Greetings,’ 1907–1912 (2013.79.1)
The Henry Ford curator’s overview of Halloween postcards and their context

note: Card descriptions are paraphrased from The Henry Ford’s object records and curator article. No postcard images or addresses are reproduced. Interpretations are labeled as readings, not documented artist intent or universal custom.

questions.prompt: A 1907–1908 card gives a watermelon wheels and uses its stem as a hand crank. What is the visual joke?
questions.context: The museum describes this as a mix of seasonal symbols and something contemporary to the card’s era. It is a comic picture, not a report of an actual machine.

options.label: The fruit is a parade float pulled by the pictured people
The stem is a handle for a harvest-field game
The card sells an actual watermelon-powered vehicle
A harvest fruit takes the place of a then-modern car

questions.explanation: The fruit and crank collide as a comic automobile. The museum describes this blend of seasonal symbols and contemporary technology; it does not document transport or advertising.

questions.prompt: The card called “Hallowe’en Precautions” puts a young woman before a mirror in a courtship fortune game. What can we responsibly read from that scene?
questions.context: The museum describes a mirror superstition, not the outcome of a prediction. The card itself dates to about 1910, which does not make the scene a record of a particular person’s future.

options.label: It documents a correct prediction for the woman pictured
It makes uncertainty about a future partner into playful suspense
It gives a practical rule for caring for mirrors
It proves every young woman used this game

questions.explanation: The scene plays with romantic fortune-telling. It supports a reading of the postcard’s joke, not a claim that the mirror worked or that everyone shared the practice.

questions.prompt: Match each museum-described card to the way it transforms an ordinary moment for Halloween.
questions.context: One shows young riders crossing a harvest field; another puts pumpkin heads on children at an apple game; a third shows a bonneted pumpkin-headed girl holding a cat beside the printed words “Sh! Ghosts!”

left.label: The riders in the harvest field
The children at the apple game

right.label: An ordinary party game gets Halloween faces
A brief whisper turns a pet into part of a staged scare
A familiar group outing becomes a night journey

questions.explanation: The hayride makes the field a route, the apple game gains pumpkin disguises, and the girl’s hush stages a small imagined fright. These are readings of described scenes, not evidence of universal customs.

questions.prompt: The watermelon card and the 1914 “Halloween Lantern” both put harvest produce in impossible travel stories. What extra job does produce do in the later card?
questions.context: In the later scene, a witch and vegetable characters ride through a harvest field under a full moon. The front of their car is a huge, glowing jack-o’-lantern face.

options.label: A jack-o’-lantern lights the travelers’ way
A pumpkin powers the car in place of its engine
A pumpkin is the only passenger in the car
A pumpkin shows the name of the road

questions.explanation: The curator says the carved jack-o’-lantern illuminates the transformed field. The earlier card turns fruit into a vehicle; this card gives produce another role in a travel story.

questions.prompt: A Clapsaddle card places a row of jolly carved pumpkins in a harvest field beneath “Curioser and Curioser.” What does the wording add?
questions.context: The museum describes carved faces and the printed greeting; it does not say the pumpkins really spoke or that an artist intended a single private meaning.

options.label: It identifies a route through the field for the reader to follow
It tells the reader how many pumpkins the grower harvested
It invites the reader to imagine the pumpkins reacting to the strange scene
It turns the image into an instruction to avoid the field

questions.explanation: The phrase gives the row of carved faces an imagined response. That is a reading of the pictured joke, separate from any documented artist intention.

questions.prompt: The 1914 lantern card bears one person’s handwritten greeting. Much later, The Henry Ford gave out reproductions and offered some copies for mailing. What link between those moments is sound?
questions.context: The museum has often given reproduction cards at its evening program since 1981 and says its Phoenixville Post Office offers reproductions for sale and mailing. A reproduction is a new copy, not the old inscribed object.

options.label: The same printed art can help different people send new personal greetings
The original writer’s exact note is sent again to its first recipient
Every surviving early card must have been mailed
Modern visitors caused the 1914 design to be printed

questions.explanation: The printed image can travel into new acts of correspondence on new copies. The museum documents the later reproductions and the old handwritten greeting without equating their individual messages.

questions.prompt: The mirror card and the “Sh! Ghosts!” cat card invite different kinds of suspense. Which comparison fits both scenes?
questions.context: In the mirror card, a woman and a man are both pictured; the museum links the scene to courtship fortune-telling. The other card shows a pumpkin-headed girl holding a cat beside “Sh! Ghosts!” Neither record verifies a prediction or a real ghost.

options.label: Both document the same future partner appearing to the girl
One proves mirror forecasts and the other proves ghosts exist
Both mainly turn a harvest fruit into a vehicle
One looks ahead to a possible relationship; the other stages a scare in the present scene

questions.explanation: The mirror story plays with uncertainty about a future relationship, even though a man is pictured. The other card’s printed words introduce a possible scare in its present scene. These are readings of the cards, not confirmation of a prophecy or ghost.

questions.prompt: A visitor calls the Clapsaddle pumpkin card “a German Halloween field” because its copy was printed in Germany. Which correction fits the record?
questions.context: The museum attributes the artwork to Ellen Clapsaddle and identifies International Art Publishing Company in the card’s production. It records Germany as the printing location, but no real location for the imagined field.

options.label: Printing in Germany proves Clapsaddle drew the card there
Printing location says where this copy was made, not where its pumpkins were pictured growing
The printing location is the place from which every copy was mailed
The field’s country can be read directly from the publisher’s name

questions.explanation: Artwork, publication, printing, and depicted setting are different facts. The catalog’s German printing field does not locate the fictional harvest field.
